profiles.label: Factory Five Racing Mk4 Roadster (Cobra replica kit, all builds)
profiles.framing: This is a home-built or shop-built fiberglass Cobra replica on a Factory Five tube-frame chassis. The builder's skill matters far more than the model year or the odometer. For a Carmel driver it is a fair-weather canyon car with no top, no airbags and real cockpit heat. The questions that decide whether it is a joy or a project are build quality, verifiable documentation, and California registration status. 'Documented and unmodified' translates here to: a known builder, a build log, receipts for every major component, and a car still close to its as-built specification.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Builder quality is the number-one failure point. Look for wiring with poor grounds, unprotected harness runs near headers, insulation-piercing splice connectors, missing fuses or relays, and fuel lines chafing on frame tubes. Ask who built it: factory/FFR-referred pro builder, independent shop, or first-time home builder. Get the build log, photos taken during assembly, and the chassis number with MSO/title. Fixing a sloppy build can run $3k–$15k+. 2) Engine-bay cooling, especially with a supercharged Coyote packed into a bay designed around a small-block. Watch for heat soak, climbing coolant temps in traffic, an undersized radiator or fan, poorly bled systems that air-lock, and supercharger intercooler pump or heat-exchanger failures. Expect $1.5k–$4k for a radiator, dual fans, shroud and intercooler pump upgrade. 3) Transmission mismatch, which is critical on a '5-speed' supercharged Coyote. A Borg-Warner/Tremec T-5 cannot survive 500–700+ lb-ft. Confirm it is a TKO-500/600, TKO-600 RR or TR-3550 and not a T-5. A TKO swap with bellhousing, input-shaft spacer and shifter is $5k–$8k. Also check driveline angles: wrong pinion or transmission angles cause vibration and U-joint wear. 4) Coyote engine items, Gen1 2011–2014 and Gen2/3 2015+. Gen1 has cam-phaser and VCT tick. Some Gen2/3 engines show oil consumption. Check the Ford Performance Control Pack or standalone ECU (Holley Terminator, etc.) for the tune file, and confirm the supercharger is matched to injector size, fuel pump and tune. Fuel-system mismatches lean out cylinders, and engine replacement is $8k–$15k. 5) Fuel system. Coyote builds need a return or regulated returnless high-flow pump. Look for fuel-tank vent and charcoal-canister issues, raw-fuel smell in the trunk or cockpit, and pinched filler necks. Pump and line corrections run $800–$2.5k. 6) Cockpit and footbox heat from side pipes and headers. Look for missing or poor heat shielding (DEI, Lizard Skin) and burned shins from side pipes. Shielding and insulation runs $500–$2k. 7) Rear suspension, which comes in three types. a) The early 4-link solid axle can bind. b) For the 3-link plus Panhard bar, check bushings and Panhard mount welds. c) For IRS cars, check the 8.8 center section mounts, CV/axle boots and toe links. Bushing or mount repairs run $500–$2.5k, and IRS center-section work runs $2k–$4k. 8) Front suspension and steering. Some kits used 1987–2004 Mustang donor spindles. Problems include bump steer from rack height, worn tie-rod ends, Coyote headers clearing the steering shaft, and manual-rack effort. An alignment and corner-weight sheet should exist. Steering corrections run $400–$1.5k. 9) Brakes. Look for a mismatched master cylinder and calipers, no adjustable proportioning valve, a soft pedal from poor bleeding, and old flex lines on older builds. Expect $500–$2k. 10) Fiberglass body and paint. Check for stress cracks and spider-webbing at door hinges, hood corners, trunk hinge points and roll-bar penetrations. Also look for gelcoat crazing, panel gaps, and stripes or clear coat that are peeling or yellowing. Spot repair costs $1k–$5k, and a respray is $10k–$20k+. 11) Chassis, roll bar and body mounting. Inspect welds at the roll-bar base and suspension pickup points, aluminum panel rivets working loose, and body-mount rubbing. Look for corrosion where powder coat has chipped. 12) Clutch hydraulics on Coyote/TKO builds. Hydraulic throwout bearings leak and are a transmission-out job, $1.2k–$2.5k. On mechanical builds, check pedal-box geometry. 13) Wheels and tires. Spinner or knock-off-style wheels must be torqued and safety-wired or clipped correctly. Many low-mile kits sit on 8–15-year-old tires that look fine but are hard and dangerous. Tires run $1k–$1.8k. 14) California registration status. A kit car without a California SB100/SPCNS title and referee label, or with an engine and supercharger combo lacking CARB compliance, may be very difficult or impossible to register in California. O

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Cooling-system upgrades if temps creep (radiator, dual fans, shroud, intercooler pump)', 'Supercharger belt, idler and tensioner replacement; intercooler fluid service', 'Clutch hydraulic or throwout-bearing service if a weep or pedal change appears', 'Suspension bushings, Panhard bar or IRS toe-link refresh', 'Additional heat shielding for footbox and side pipes', 'Fiberglass stress-crack repair and paint touch-up at hinge points', 'Spark plugs and coil checks on a boosted Coyote (gapped per tune)', 'Exhaust gasket and side-pipe mount repairs; leak checks']
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven mainly by builder reputation, drivetrain and paint quality, not mileage or year. Coyote 5.0 (supercharged carries a premium) and well-sorted 302/347/427W builds lead the market, with LS builds slightly behind. A TKO-600 or similar transmission is expected, and a T-5 behind big power is a discount. IRS and later 3-link chassis bring more than early 4-link cars. Show-quality paint with classic stripe combinations (Guardsman Blue/white, black/silver) adds value, and a full build log with receipts adds a lot. In California, a clean SB100/SPCNS title can be worth thousands over an out-of-state-only title. Typical driver-quality builds trade at roughly $35k–$60k, and pro-built supercharged Coyote cars $65k–$90k+.
profiles.catchup_notes: Kit cars often have low miles but long sit times. Expect aged tires, dried brake fluid, stale fuel effects, and hardened rubber in hoses and bushings even on a 'fresh' build. Budget for a thorough shakedown that re-torques every fastener and sorts the builder's loose ends (wiring, heat, cooling) before treating the car as a reliable driver.

profiles.label: Ford Bronco (First Generation, 1966–1977 "Early Bronco")
profiles.framing: For this buyer the early Bronco is a weekend-and-errand toy that has to actually drive to Big Sur, Laureles Grade, and the beach without drama — not a trailer queen and not a show car. Because almost none survive unmodified, the realistic goal is a documented, coherently built truck: rust-free structure, one shop's fingerprints on the driveline, and receipts that explain every deviation from stock. The single biggest determinant of long-term cost is metal — body mounts, frame rails at the shock towers, rear quarters and floors — followed by whether the builder solved the known weak links (steering, brakes, cooling, wiring, fuel) or just bolted on lift and tires. A restomod with a crate engine and an overdrive-less or freshly rebuilt automatic is acceptable here; an undocumented 'built motor' with mystery fabrication is not.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rust is the defining issue and it is structural, not cosmetic. Check the rear quarter panels and inner wheel arches, the floor pans (especially under the driver's-side fuel tank on 1966–77 trucks that retain the under-seat tank), the tailgate skin and its lower corners, the rear crossmember, the windshield frame lower corners, and the cowl/kick panel area. Full quarter replacement with blend paint runs $3,000–$8,000 per side; a body-off metal restoration is $60,000–$150,000. Look for panel-gap irregularity, seam sealer that hides filler, and magnet/thickness-gauge evidence.", "Frame and body-mount corrosion. The front frame rails rot at the shock-tower/coil-spring mounts and at the radius-arm rear mounts; cracks propagate there from lift and oversize tires. Rotted body mounts let the tub shift and the doors stop closing. Weld-in frame stiffeners or repair plates are common and should be documented — new mounts and rail repair is $1,500–$5,000 of labor. Get clear underbody photos, not just 'no rust' claims.", '\'Bronco lean\' and worn front suspension. Sagging driver-side coil spring, tired radius-arm bushings, and a worn track bar / drag-link joint produce lean, wander, and shimmy-into-death-wobble at 45–60 mph, badly amplified by 33s and a 2.5" lift. Springs, bushings, shocks, and a full front end joint refresh is $1,200–$3,000; lifts done without correcting steering geometry or drop pitman arm create permanent bump steer.', 'Steering. Factory 1966–75 Ross cam-and-lever box (manual, or the weak Saginaw power box later) is vague and leaks; most good builds convert to a Saginaw power box or Borgeson unit with a new pitman arm and a hydraulic ram or quick-ratio setup. Verify the conversion is bolted through reinforced frame metal — cracked steering-box frame mounts are a known failure. Conversion cost $1,200–$2,500. Excessive on-center play or a leak at the box should be priced in.', 'Brakes. Front drums through 1975 (discs standard 1976–77) are marginal for modern traffic with big tires. Disc conversions (Wilwood/TOMS/Wild Horses, often with hydroboost) are common and desirable but must include a correct proportioning valve and sized master cylinder — symptoms of a bad job are long pedal travel, rear lockup, or no boost. Budget $1,500–$3,000 for a proper four-wheel disc/hydroboost job and inspect for fresh, correctly routed hard lines and a non-weeping booster.', "Fuel system. The original under-seat tank and sending units are a chronic problem: failing fuel gauges, cracked rubber fill hoses, weeping sender flanges, and fire risk from decades-old rubber lines under the cab. This listing's June 2026 sender and gauge replacement is exactly the typical item. A rear-tank relocation plus new lines and a properly rated in-tank pump for EFI is $800–$2,500; on EFI conversions, confirm return line, pump rating, and pressure regulator install quality.", 'Wiring and grounds. Original harnesses are brittle, the bulkhead connector and headlight/ignition switches overheat, and gauges read erratically. A complete American Autowire/Painless harness with a modern fuse box (as here) is a major plus; verify it was actually finished — look for loose splices, unfused add-ons, and LED-light or winch circuits tapped off the ignition. A proper rewire is $900–$1,500 in parts plus 20–40 hours labor.', 'Cooling. The stock radiator and shroudless fan are marginal; anything with a 302/347 stroker, big tires, and A/C or a body lift will run hot in stop-and-go or on a grade. Look for an aluminum crossflow radiator, correct shroud, and an electric fan setup with a proper relay. A 415 hp stroker in a 3,500-lb truck with 35s will also cook the transmission without an auxiliary cooler — confirm one exists.', "Drivetrain leaks and driveline angles. The Dana 20 transfer case seeps at the rear output seal and the shifter/housing gasket; twin-stick conversions can leak or pop out of gear if the detents and shift rails aren't right. Lifted trucks commonly vibrate f
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Replace tires — 2010 date codes are unsafe regardless of tread; a set of 33"–35" Toyo/BFG plus mount, balance, and alignment is $1,600–$2,400.', 'Full fluid service: engine oil, trans fluid and filter (fresh look at the rebuilt 4R70W), transfer case, both differentials, brake fluid flush, coolant.', 'Front-end inspection and retorque: radius arm bolts, track bar, drag link, tie rod ends, steering box mount, pitman arm nut; set toe and caster for the lift ($300–$800).', 'Brake system verification: bed-in, check hydroboost/master for weeping, confirm proportioning valve adjustment and parking brake function ($200–$600).', 'Chase leaks and finish-work items typical of a fresh build: fabricated engine mount inspection, exhaust hanger/clearance, fuel line routing and clamps, EFI fuel pressure
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Driveline vibration resolution if any remains: pinion angle shims, carrier bearing, or re-balance of the rear shaft ($400–$1,200).', 'Dana 20 rear output seal and shifter housing reseal; front axle knuckle/hub seal service ($600–$1,500).', 'EFI/ignition tuning and drivability sorting on the Sniper (idle, cold start, timing curve) plus possible distributor or coil work ($400–$1,000).', 'Seat, top, and weatherseal work: soft-top fit, windshield seam leak, door seals, and possible hardtop acquisition or refresh ($500–$3,000).', 'Cosmetic touch-in of documented chips/scratches on the tailgate and rear bumper corner; underbody cavity wax/rust-proofing given coastal Carmel air ($800–$2,000).', 'Gearing/final-drive reassessment if the truck feels under-geared on 35s, or a rear axle service if w
profiles.market_notes: Value is driven first by structure and documentation, then by build quality and taste: a rust-free, receipt-backed truck from a known builder (Icon, Gateway, Velocity, Kincer, TOMS/Wild Horses parts done well) sells far above a nice-looking backyard build. Uncut, original-spec 1966–68 examples — especially roadsters, Sports, and 1971–75 4-speed/V8 wagons with a Marti Report — command originality money, while tastefully executed restomods with fuel injection, four-wheel discs, power steering, and a modern overdrive automatic trade in a wide $45,000–$120,000 band. Color matters (factory-correct Brittany Blue, Wimbledon White, Boxwood Green read better than trendy repaints), as does a matching hardtop plus soft top; a color change away from the Marti-documented original costs some money with purists. Odometer readings are irrelevant; 'documented restoration with invoices in the gallery' is worth real dollars, and undocumented 415 hp claims are worth a discount.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a freshly restored early Bronco needs a first-year sorting budget: 50-year-old rubber and hardware (tires, seals, hoses, body mounts, weatherstrip) and the inevitable punch-list of a recent build — leaks, fuel and wiring finish work, driveline angles, and brake/steering bedding. Assume everything not on a receipt is original and due, and add coastal rust-prevention (cavity wax, underbody treatment) immediately given Carmel's salt air.

profiles.label: Honda CR-V (1st gen RD1, 1997-2001)
profiles.framing: A first-gen CR-V is a simple, durable, Civic-based compact utility. Here it serves as a practical coastal daily for Carmel and an easy-to-wrench beach and Big Sur hauler. It is not an off-roader: Real Time 4WD is a reactive rear-pump system with no low range. Condition matters more than mileage, specifically rust, oil consumption, timing belt history and rear-diff fluid care. A documented, unmodified, rust-free manual 4WD example is the target, and it must pass California smog without an expensive CARB-compliant catalytic converter.
profiles.weak_points: ["Timing belt is an interference-engine wear item. The B20B (1997-98, 126 hp) and B20Z (1999-2001, 146 hp) are both interference designs. Honda's interval is 105k miles or about 7 years, and on these cars age is usually the deciding factor. A snapped belt bends valves, and the repair often exceeds the car's value. Do the water pump, tensioner, cam and crank seals, and drive belts at the same time, for about $700-1,200. Ask for a dated receipt with the odometer reading. A sticker on the belt cover alone is not enough.", 'B20 oil consumption is a known trait. Stuck or worn low-tension oil control rings can burn a quart every 500-1,500 miles. Symptoms are blue smoke on cold start or after idling, oily or fouled plugs, and a sooty tailpipe. Ring and rebuild work runs $2,500-4,500, or about $2,500-3,500 for a used engine swap. Watch the cold-start video for smoke. Ask how often the owner adds oil. Ask for a compression test, and a leak-down test if compression is borderline.', 'Real Time 4WD rear differential depends on its fluid. The dual-pump rear diff needs genuine Honda Dual Pump Fluid (DPSF / DPF II) changed roughly every 30k miles or 3 years. Neglected or wrong fluid causes groaning, shudder or binding on tight low-speed turns such as parking lots and U-turns. A fluid change is $80-150 and often cures it. A worn clutch pack or failed pump runs $600-1,500 used, or more for a rebuild. Mismatched tire sizes or wear between axles also stresses the system. Ask for diff fluid receipts.', 'The 4-speed automatic (only transmission in 1997; optional thereafter) is more robust than later Honda automatics but not immune. Look for flare between 2-3 or 3-4, harsh engagement, and torque-converter lockup shudder. These issues are often worse with non-Honda ATF; it should be Z1, now superseded by DW-1. A used unit installed costs $1,500-2,500 and a rebuild $2,500-3,500. Look for regular drain-and-fill records, and check that the ATF is red rather than brown or burnt-smelling.', 'On the 5-speed manual (1998+ in the US, the desirable spec), check for 2nd and 3rd gear synchro grind when shifted quickly, especially if non-Honda gear oil was used. Honda MTF is correct. Also check for a high or slipping clutch engagement and leaks at the clutch master or slave cylinder. A clutch job runs $900-1,400. Synchro repair means a transmission rebuild, $1,500-2,500, or a used unit.', 'Rust is the main killer of these cars. Check the rear wheel arches and quarter-panel lips, rocker panels behind the plastic cladding, rear subframe and trailing-arm mounts, spare-tire carrier and swing gate lower edge, and floor pan seams. Coastal Carmel fog and salt air keep working on any existing rust. Washington, Northeast and Midwest cars may have seen road salt. Structural rust at the trailing-arm or subframe mounts is a walk-away. Get underbody photos or a lift inspection.', 'The swing-out rear door and its hinges sag over time from the weight of the full-size spare. The result is a rubbing latch, hard closing, rattles, and water leaks into the cargo floor well. Hinge pins and bushings or an adjustment run $100-400. Look for water staining or rust under the cargo picnic table and in the spare well.', 'Ignition distributor problems are common. The igniter or ignition coil inside the Hitachi/TEC distributor fails with heat, causing a hot no-start or stalling. The distributor shaft O-ring leaks oil onto the block. Cap and rotor wear out. A remanufactured distributor is $150-400 in parts. Worn plug wires and cap cause misfires that can fail a California smog test.', "The PGM-FI main relay is a classic Honda hot no-start. Its solder joints crack, so the engine cranks but won't start on hot days, then starts after cooling. Resoldering is cheap and a new relay is $40-100. It is worth carrying a spare.", 'Idle and emissions control parts age out. Watch for a fast-idle thermo valve or IAC valve causing high or hunting idle, a clogged EGR passage on the B20Z, aging upstream and

profiles.market_notes: Prices for clean examples have risen sharply. Documented low-mileage manual 4WD cars now reach $10k-15k+ at enthusiast auctions, while average automatics with 150k+ miles trade around $3k-7k. Value is driven by the 5-speed manual, 4WD, a rust-free underbody, originality (paint, steelies or factory alloys, no lift or aftermarket wheels), mileage under about 100k, and a recent timing belt receipt. The EX adds alloys and ABS, and the 2001 SE adds leather and body-color trim. Desirable colors include Tahitian Green, Supermarine Blue, Clover Green and Taffeta White. Single-owner documented cars carry a meaningful premium over unknown-history examples.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most surviving RD1s are 25+ years old and due for a rubber refresh regardless of mileage: timing belt, hoses, mounts, bushings, CV boots and tires. Many also need a full fluid reset with Honda-specific fluids. Budget about $1,500-3,500 to bring a typical undocumented example to a reliable baseline, and more if rust repair or a CARB-compliant catalytic converter is needed.

profiles.label: Honda Civic Type R (EK9)
profiles.framing: The EK9 is the purest expression of the B-series VTEC formula: ~1,060 kg, a hand-ported 8,400-rpm B16B, a helical LSD, a seam-welded shell, and a 5-speed with the best shift feel Honda ever built. For a Carmel-based driver it is a weekend Highway 1 / Laureles Grade toy that can also do a grocery run, not a daily commuter — no airbag-era safety margin, RHD on US roads, and grey-market parts logistics. What matters most for this buyer is that the car is a genuine, unbutchered EK9 (correct VIN prefix, correct chassis, matching-spec engine) with an honest Japanese auction sheet and a clean, documented US import; cosmetics and bolt-on mods matter far less than shell integrity, theft/VIN history, and whether the engine has been thrashed or swapped. Because these are now 25+ year old imports, the realistic goal is a sorted, documented driver, not a museum piece — but a car with a fabricated chassis story or hidden structural repair is worth far less than the bid suggests.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Identity and import legitimacy: real EK9s carry an EK9-1xxxxxx VIN and a B16B with '00' cylinder-head casting and a specific engine number range. Cloned EK4/EK3/EG shells wearing EK9 badges and B16A engines are a persistent problem, as are stolen/recovered Japanese cars and 'VIN-swapped' shells. Demand the Japanese export certificate (deregistration/'matsusho' document), the auction sheet, the US Customs HS-7/EPA 3520-1 and DOT HS-7 25-year exemption paperwork, the bill of lading, and the US title — and verify the chassis-plate VIN against the paperwork and the stamped firewall/strut-tower number. A wrong or restamped VIN is a walk-away, not a discount.

2) Front-end structural repair: EK9s in Japan were raced and crashed. Replaced radiator core support, replaced hood, aftermarket bumper and non-OEM fenders (exactly the pattern in this listing) usually mean a front hit. Check frame-rail creases behind the bumper beam, seam-sealer disturbance at the rail-to-apron welds, overspray in the engine bay, and mismatched panel gaps. Also confirm the EK9-specific factory seam welding along the strut towers and floor seams is intact — a shell repaired by a Japanese body shop with a donor front clip is common. Proper frame straightening plus OEM panels is $3,000–$8,000; a car already 'repaired' badly is a permanent value hit of $3k–$6k.

3) Rust: JDM cars from snow-belt or coastal Japan rust at the rear wheel-arch lips, the rear quarter behind the arch, the rear subframe/trailing-arm mounting points, the front strut tower tops, the battery tray and fuel-filler neck area, and the rear beam pockets under the spare tire well. Undercoating/'Wax-oyl' sprayed by an importer is often hiding pitting. Budget $1,500–$5,000 for proper arch/quarter repair; structural rust at the rear suspension mounts is a dealbreaker.

4) B16B timing belt, water pump and tensioner: 90k-mile/7-year interval, and an interference engine. A B-pillar sticker or Japanese shaken record is only weak evidence. Want a receipt with belt, tensioner, idler, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance-shaft-free (B16B has no balance shafts) done together — $700–$1,200 at an independent Honda specialist. A snapped belt is an $3,500–$6,000 rebuild.

5) VTEC and valvetrain wear at 90k+ miles: sticking VTEC spool valve / clogged screen causing a P1259 or no upper-cam engagement, noisy exhaust-side rocker, and worn valve guides on cars run hard with long oil intervals. Valve lash must be set every 30k; ticking at idle is normal Honda, harshness plus smoke on overrun is not. Leakdown on all four cylinders is mandatory — healthy is under 8%. A tired B16B that won't pull cleanly to 8,400 rpm means either a top-end refresh ($2,500–$4,000) or an honest rebuild ($5,000–$8,000).

6) Distributor and ignition: OEM TD-series distributor leaks oil from the O-ring into the cap, the internal ignition coil and igniter fail with heat, and the crank/cyl-position sensors inside the distributor cause intermittent no-starts and high-rpm misfires. A genuine Honda distributor is now $400–$700; rebuild kits and no-name units are a common cheap fix that fails again.

7) Engine oil leaks and seals: valve cover gasket and spark plug tube seals, distributor O-ring, oil pan gasket, front and rear main seals, and the VTEC solenoid gasket. On a 25-year-old car expect at least two of these. Individually cheap ($150–$500 each), collectively a $1,000 day.

8) S4C transmission and helical LSD: 3rd- and 5th-gear synchro wear (crunch on fast 2-3 upshifts), and on abused cars worn LSD gears or a whining final drive. Clutch life on a hard-driven EK9 is 50k–80k miles; clutch, pressure plate, release bearing and resurfaced flywheel is $900–$1,500. A rebuilt S4C with LSD is $2,500–$4,500, and a correct EK9 LSD transaxle is getting scarce — a car with an EK4/EG swap transaxle loses the LSD and real value.

9) Suspension and bushings: almost every EK9 has been on coilovers (Tein, Buddy Club, etc.) for decades. Expect blow
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (Honda MTF in the transaxle, correct 10W-30/0W-40, coolant, brake fluid flush); timing belt/water pump/tensioner unless a verifiable receipt with parts and date exists; compression and leakdown-driven decisions; replace valve cover gasket, plug tube seals and distributor O-ring; new OEM-spec plugs, wires, cap and rotor (or full distributor if it leaks or misfires); set valve lash; four matching correct-size tires (185/60R14 or 195/55R15 depending on wheel) — the listing's mismatched 185/65 and 195/55 pairs must all be replaced immediately; full alignment after correcting ride height; brake pads/rotors and caliper slide service; wheel bearings if humming; A/C diagnosis and repair or a decision to live without it; sort or remove any hack alarm/immobilizer wiring. Realistic
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and transmission fluid/synchro assessment, likely clutch job; replacement of tired coilovers with a known damper set plus new top mounts, ball joints, tie rods, and front/rear bushings; radiator, hoses and thermostat if original; fuel pump and filter on a car that sat; exhaust system returned to a quieter, hanger-correct setup; Recaro bolster repair or retrim; replacement of broken climate vents and cracked mirror housing with OEM-used JDM parts; sourcing and fitting the correct EK9 front lip, fenders and hood if the front-end repair was done with non-OEM panels; rust remediation at rear arches and undercarriage with a proper cavity wax treatment for coastal Carmel air. Expect $3,000–$7,000 depending on how much of the front-end and suspension story needs undoing.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by authenticity and chassis honesty: a documented, accident-free, low-kilometer EK9 with the Japanese auction sheet, export certificate, and clean US title trades far above a repaired or clone car. Championship White is the iconic and most valuable color and typically commands a 15–25% premium over Flamenco Black Pearl, Sunlight Yellow (99/00 facelift), and Milano Red; the 1999–2000 facelift with the optional A/C and audio package is slightly preferred as a usable car. Originality of the drivetrain (matching B16B and the LSD-equipped S4C transaxle), intact factory seam welds, unmolested engine bay, and the presence of original Recaros, wheels, wheel, shift knob and front lip move money meaningfully; heavy mods, missing trim, mismatched tires and dead A/C are discounts but also leverage. Under ~$15k in 2024–25 usually signals a repaired shell, unverifiable history, or a dealer flip of a fresh import with no PPI — good, honest examples sit in the $25k–$45k range and exceptional low-km cars go higher.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any 25-year-old JDM import as needing a full deferred-maintenance reset: timing belt/water pump, all seals and gaskets, every rubber hose and bushing, fuel pump and filter, brake and clutch hydraulics, and a complete fluid change regardless of what the seller claims. Coilovers and exhaust fitted a decade ago in Japan are consumables that are almost certainly finished. Budget $4,000–$7,000 in the first year purely to bring a driver-grade EK9 back to a known, safe baseline before spending anything on cosmetics.

profiles.label: Infiniti FX50 (S51, 2009-2013)
profiles.framing: The S51 FX50 is a 390-hp V8 performance crossover built on Nissan's FM platform. For a Carmel driver it is a comfortable, quick, all-weather daily and weekend car that is at home on Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and occasional Tahoe runs. It has real cargo utility but is not an off-roader, and expect roughly 14-17 mpg on premium fuel. The core drivetrain is robust. The risks are in the aging interior materials, the complex chassis electronics (especially on Sport-package cars), and a 7-speed automatic that Nissan called 'lifetime fill'. Prioritize documented fluid service and a clean full-module scan over trim level.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Dashboard bubbling and delamination: the soft-touch upper dash on S51 FX (and related G/M/EX interiors of the era) is well known for bubbling, lifting, and turning sticky, typically around the defroster area, above the center screen, and above the glovebox. Heat and UV make it worse, and it shows up at any mileage by year 8-10. Look for repairs or patching (as seen in the example listing's comments), dash covers hiding damage, and any record of an Infiniti goodwill or extended-coverage replacement. A proper dash panel replacement runs roughly $1,500-3,500 installed; a professional reskin runs $600-1,200.

2) Electronic steering column lock (ESCL): the Nissan/Infiniti ESCL of this era can fail to disengage, causing a no-start condition with a steering-lock warning, often intermittent at first. Nissan issued service campaigns and bulletins for this family of cars. Ask for campaign completion or an ESCL replacement or reprogramming record. Out-of-pocket cost is roughly $400-1,200.

3) 7-speed automatic (Jatco JR710E/RE7R01A): marketed as lifetime fill, but fluid degraded past 60-80k miles can bring harsh 2-3 or 3-4 shifts, flare on upshift, delayed engagement, or torque-converter shudder. Valve body or solenoid faults also occur. Look for Matic S (or approved equivalent) drain-and-fills with receipts every 30-60k. Valve body work runs $1,200-2,500; a rebuild or replacement runs $4,000-7,000.

4) VK50VE V8 oil leaks: the engine is often misprinted in listings as 'VQ50VE' and is the VK-family V8. It is generally durable. Common age items are valve cover gaskets and spark-plug tube seals, which leak oil into the plug wells and cause misfires, plus seepage at the timing chain cover and oil cooler. Valve cover gaskets run $700-1,400 per pair with labor. Timing cover resealing is $1,500+.

5) VVEL, timing chain, and exhaust manifold: the VVEL (variable valve event and lift) system on the intake side can throw control-shaft sensor or actuator codes (P1090-P1093-type families). Chain rattle or guide wear can appear on engines run on long oil-change intervals. Exhaust manifold ticking from cracks or gasket leaks, a known VK-family trait, is worth listening for cold. VVEL actuator or controller work runs $800-2,000; exhaust manifolds run $800-2,000 per side.

6) Rear Active Steer (RAS), Sport-package cars: the rear-steer actuator and its control module can fail or leak, setting a warning light and making rear-end handling feel odd. The actuator runs $1,500-3,000 installed; used units are an option.

7) Continuous Damping Control (CDC) adaptive dampers, Sport package: the electronically adjustable shocks leak or fault with age and are expensive, roughly $600-1,200 per corner OEM. Some owners convert to passive dampers, which the buyer should treat as a modification.

8) ATTESA E-TS AWD transfer case and differentials: the electronically controlled transfer clutch and the front and rear diffs are frequently never serviced. Watch for AWD warning lights, binding in tight parking-lot turns, or whine. Fluid services are cheap ($150-400). A transfer case or diff replacement runs $1,500-3,500.

9) Front suspension wear: this is a heavy car, and the standard 21-inch wheels make it harder on parts. Front lower control arm compliance bushings, rear upper arms, and sway-bar links wear by 60-90k, causing clunks, brake shimmy, and uneven tire wear. Arms and bushings run $600-1,500 plus an alignment.

10) Wheels and tires: 265/45R21 tires cost $1,200-2,000 per set, and the rims bend and curb easily. Check tire date codes, since low-mileage cars often have 8+ year-old tires. Straightening or refinishing a wheel runs $150-300.

11) Brakes: this 4,300-lb car goes through pads and rotors fairly quickly and can develop pulsation from warped or overheated rotors. Expect $600-1,200 per axle for OEM-quality parts.

12) HID and AFS adaptive headlights: xenon bulbs, ballasts, and the swivel motors in the adaptive front lighting system (AFS) fail with age. Lens

profiles.market_notes: The FX50 was produced in small numbers and carries a meaningful premium over FX35/FX37 examples. Low-mileage, one-owner, documented cars sit at the top of the market, roughly $20-25k in 2026 (the example sold at $23,500 with 41k miles). Typical 80-120k-mile cars trade far lower. Technology and Deluxe Touring equipment adds value, and Sport-package cars (CDC, RAS, sport seats) appeal to enthusiasts but carry higher repair exposure. 2012-2013 refresh cars are marginally preferred. Dash condition, documented transmission service, and a clean scan move price more than color. Black Obsidian and dark interiors are common; lighter interiors show dash and wear issues more visibly.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 2009-2013 FX50s treated the transmission, transfer case, and differential fluids as lifetime-fill and are due for driveline fluid catch-up, plus coolant, brake fluid, and aged tires, even at low miles. At 13-17 years old, expect to address rubber bushings, valve cover and plug tube seals, HID components, and dash material condition within the first year. Budget about $1,500-3,000 of catch-up on a typical example beyond the risk reserve.

profiles.label: International Harvester Scout II (incl. Traveler, Terra, SSII)
profiles.framing: This is a hand-built-feeling, body-on-frame 1970s 4x4 that the buyer will drive on the Monterey Peninsula, Carmel Valley Road, and the occasional beach/fire-road run — not a garage queen and not a stock-market substitute. What matters most is metal: a Scout II is essentially a rust-and-documentation purchase wrapped around a very simple, very rebuildable drivetrain. Mechanicals (304/345 V8, TF727 or T-19, Dana 20, Dana 44s) are cheap and well-supported by the aftermarket; a rotten rear quarter, floor, or frame rail is what turns a $29k truck into a $50k truck. Because coastal California air is hard on these, a Scout that has lived near the ocean without proper undercarriage care should be judged more harshly than mileage or cosmetics would suggest.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rear quarter panels and the rear 'kick-up' area behind the rear wheels are the classic Scout II rot zone — the inner/outer quarter sandwich and the rear wheelhouse trap mud and never dry out. Any car described as having 'some typical Scout rust' should be assumed to have this. Proper cut-and-weld repair with quality reproduction panels runs $3,000–$8,000 per side once paint blending is included; bondo-and-fiberglass patches are common and disqualifying at this price point.", 'Floor pans, footwells, and the seat-belt/seat-mount reinforcements rust from the top down (leaking windshield gasket, cowl vent, and door seals) and from the bottom up. Pull the carpet or mats; look for fresh undercoating or seam sealer hiding perforation. Floor pan replacement $1,500–$3,500.', 'Frame: the boxed rails are usually decent but rot at the rear spring hangers, the rear crossmember, and where the body mounts perch. Body mount bushings (12 points) collapse and let the tub shift, causing door-gap and hood-alignment weirdness. New mount kit $150–$400 in parts, a full day of labor; frame rail section repair $2,000–$5,000 and a value cliff.', 'Tailgate, rear hatch/glass frame, and the tailgate lower channel rot from the inside out; drain holes plug. A good used or repro tailgate is $600–$1,500 and often needs paint.', 'Windshield frame, cowl, and A-pillar corners: the windshield surround rusts under the gasket and leaks into the cowl and kick panels. Repair means glass out and welding — $1,500–$3,000 with glass and paint.', "Engines: the IH 304/345/392 V8s are torquey and durable but low-compression and thirsty (10–13 mpg). Common issues are cracked exhaust manifolds, hardened valve stem seals (blue smoke on startup), rear main seepage, and timing chain stretch past ~90k. Parts supply is aftermarket-dependent (IH Parts America, Super Scout Specialists, Scout Light Line); a full rebuild is $5,000–$8,000. Ask for a compression/leakdown record, not just 'runs great'.", 'Fuel system: the original Holley 2210/2300-series two-barrel is finicky and often replaced with a Motorcraft 2100 or Edelbrock. Original dual side-mounted fuel tanks rust, sending units fail, and the selector valve and steel lines corrode — expect $600–$1,500 to sort tanks, lines, pump, and sender. Sniff for gas smell in the cabin and under the rear.', "Cooling: 304 + TF727 combinations run hot in traffic; original radiators, fan clutches, and rotted heater cores are common. 'New radiator' is a good sign but confirm the fan clutch, shroud (often missing), water pump, and hoses were done as a system — $600–$1,200 for the rest.", 'Electrical: 40+ year old harnesses go brittle behind the dash and at the bulkhead/engine bay connectors; ammeter-based charging circuits, headlight switch, and turn-signal switch are common failure points and a real fire risk. Look for a documented harness replacement or at minimum clean, non-crispy, non-Scotch-locked wiring. Full harness $1,500–$3,000 installed. Points/Prestolite ignition is usually (and sensibly) converted to Pertronix or HEI.', 'Steering: Saginaw box wear, worn steering shaft rag joint, sagging Pitman/idler geometry and worn tie rod/drag link ends give the famous Scout wander. A rebuilt box plus full linkage rebuild is $1,200–$2,500 and transforms the truck. Also check the steering column mount and the frame-side box mounting area for cracks.', 'Brakes: front discs from 1974-on, drums prior; master cylinders, rubber flex lines, rear wheel cylinders, and the vacuum booster all age out. Sticky rear drums and a long pedal are typical. Full system refresh $1,200–$2,500. Confirm the parking brake actually works.', 'Drivetrain: the Chrysler TF727 automatic and T-19/T-428 four-speeds are stout; the Dana 20 transfer case leaks from the rear seal and gets sloppy shift detents. Dana 44 front (closed knuckle on early, later units too) and Dana 44/Dana 60 rear are strong, but front axle U-joints, knuckle seals, and wheel bearings are frequently overdue
profiles.immediate_repairs: Assume a full fluid and filter service (engine, TF727 with pan drop and filter, Dana 20, both diffs, brake fluid flush), all rubber brake flex lines plus a master cylinder, a carb rebuild or Motorcraft 2100 swap with fresh fuel filter and rubber lines, ignition tune (cap/rotor/wires/plugs or a Pertronix/HEI conversion), full steering linkage inspection with tie rod ends and rag joint as needed, new door/window/tailgate weatherstrip and a windshield gasket reseal, body mount bushing replacement, and battery/charging cleanup including the ammeter circuit. Budget $2,500–$5,000 at an independent shop, less if you do it yourself.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Expect a Saginaw steering box rebuild and possibly a steering shaft, front axle U-joints and knuckle/wheel bearing service, a cooling system round-out (water pump, fan clutch, shroud, heater core), exhaust from the manifolds back including cracked manifold repair, fuel tank and sender work, seat foam and interior trim, and localized rust repair on the rear quarters/floor once you know how deep the 'typical Scout rust' really goes. $4,000–$9,000 is realistic; a proper quarter-panel and floor job alone can eat all of it.
profiles.market_notes: Values are driven almost entirely by metal quality, documentation, and how honest the presentation is: a rust-free Arizona/California truck with the original line-setting ticket and receipts can be double a rusty one with identical mileage. Traveler and Terra long-wheelbase bodies and SSII/Rallye trim carry premiums, as do factory 345/392 V8s, four-speed manuals, factory A/C, and desirable two-tone paint; automatics are normal and not a penalty on a truck like this. Mileage matters far less than a documented engine/trans rebuild and evidence of professional rust repair. At $29k the market expects either a solid, well-documented driver or a truck with clearly disclosed and quantified rust — 'some typical Scout rust' with no photos is a price-negotiation lever, not a description.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 45-year-old Scout II that has not had a documented recommissioning needs the full age-related sweep regardless of mileage: all rubber (brake lines, fuel lines, coolant hoses, weatherstrip, body mounts, suspension bushings), the wiring harness assessed for brittleness, and every fluid changed. Assume $3,000–$6,000 of catch-up in year one on a good example, and treat any 'some typical rust' language as an open-ended line item until you have seen it on a lift.

profiles.label: Jeep Wrangler JK / JK Unlimited (2007–2018, incl. Rubicon & Rubicon X)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the JK Unlimited Rubicon is a dual-purpose tool: a Monterey-Peninsula daily that can run Los Padres fire roads, haul bikes and dogs, and go to the desert without drama. The Rubicon hardware (Rock-Trac 4:1, Tru-Lok front and rear lockers, electric sway-bar disconnect, Dana 44 front) is the reason to buy this trim rather than a Sport, and a 2014 gets the sorted 3.6 Pentastar plus the NSG370 six-speed. Because Wranglers are the most-modified vehicle in America, the real job is separating a documented, thoughtfully built truck from a bar-crawled parts-catalog project — and, in California, confirming the thing can actually be registered and smogged. Value here lives in records, geometry that doesn't shake, and a frame/underbody that hasn't been eaten by salt.
profiles.weak_points: 1) 3.6 Pentastar left-bank cylinder head (2011–early 2013 builds, worst before the revised casting): valve-seat/guide failure shows as cold ticking, misfire on cylinder 2 or 4, P0300/P0302/P0304 and a rough idle; head replacement is $2,500–$4,500. Chrysler extended coverage to 7yr/70k on many, so look for a dealer head-replacement invoice or confirm the engine build/casting date. A 2014 is largely past this, but any ticking deserves a compression/leak-down. 2) Oil filter housing / oil cooler assembly (plastic, Pentastar, ~60k+): cracks and warps, leaking oil down the rear of the block and coolant into the oil cooler; symptoms are oil smell, drips onto the exhaust, sometimes overheating. Aluminum aftermarket or updated Mopar unit, $500–$1,200 installed. If a seller claims it was done, get the invoice — this is the single most common Pentastar leak. 3) Death wobble: violent front-end oscillation after hitting a bump at 45–65 mph, caused by worn track bar bushings/bolt hole, loose track bar at the axle bracket, worn Dana 44 ball joints, or a poorly geometried lift. Ball joints are consumables at 60k–100k on lifted, big-tire trucks; $600–$1,400 per axle. Look for recent track bar, ball joint, and alignment receipts (the example listing shows lower ball joints at 92k — good sign, but ask what was left). 4) Steering box sector-shaft play and loose steering: vague on-center feel, clunk on turn-in; boxes wear at 80k–120k, often accelerated by 35s. Box $600–$1,200; a steering stabilizer is a band-aid, not a fix — a Falcon/adjustable stabilizer on a lifted JK can mask underlying wobble. 5) Frame and body rust: the JK frame rots at the rear lower control arm mounts, the skid plate/crossmember area, and around the rear body mounts and shock towers; door hinges, tailgate hinge, and windshield frame corners bubble. New-England/salt-belt cars (this example is NH-titled) need a lift-and-poke inspection with a screwdriver — perforation at a control arm mount is a structural repair, $2,000–$5,000 or a walk-away. 6) Water leaks: Freedom Top panel seals, hardtop-to-windshield and side-rail seals, door surrounds, and cowl drains all leak, soaking carpet and rusting the floor pan and seat brackets. Pull carpet edges and check for mud/moisture; sound-deadening foam installed under carpet (as here) can hide standing water. 7) NSG370 six-speed: notchy cold shifting is normal, but grinding into 3rd/4th, a heavy or dragging clutch, and a leaking or spongy hydraulic clutch slave (integral throwout bearing) are not. Clutch + slave is a transmission-out job, $1,500–$2,800. Fluid is a specific MTX spec and almost never changed. 8) Cooling and gaskets: plastic-tank radiators seep at 80k–120k ($400–$800), thermostat housing and water pump leak, and 3.6 valve cover/rear main seeps are common at high mileage. 9) TIPM / electrical gremlins (2011–2013 especially): fuel pump relay failure causing no-start or stalling, wipers or horn acting up; a bad TIPM is $600–$1,300. Also window regulators/motors, blend door actuators (clicking behind dash), and radio/Uconnect 730N nav units that fail or lose touch response ($400–$900 used/refurb). 10) Driveline vibration on lifted trucks: a 3.5" lift needs correct pinion angle, often front/rear driveshaft replacement (Adams shafts here are the right answer) and a slip-yoke/exhaust clearance check; leftover vibration usually means transfer case output seal wear, worn u-joints, or a bad rear main drive flange. 11) Exhaust manifold studs/bolts and heat shield rattle on Pentastars; broken studs cause a cold-start tick that mimics head failure. 12) Axles under big tires: front unit bearings (wheel hubs) go at 70k–120k with play/hum ($250–$450 each), Tru-Lok locker wiring and actuator connectors at the axle corrode and throw locker faults, and front axle inner C / knuckle wear shows up on rock-crawled trucks. 13) Gearing mismatch: stock 4.10s with 35s or larger without a regear makes the truck slow, hurts mpg, and increases clutch a
profiles.immediate_repairs: Tires (anything with 2015–2017 date codes is expired regardless of tread — five 35" DuraTracs mounted/balanced, $1,300–$1,900); full four-corner front-end inspection and re-torque/replace of track bar, ball joints, tie rod ends and drag link as needed ($400–$1,500); four-wheel alignment with caster set for the lift; oil filter housing/cooler inspection and replacement if the original plastic unit or if leaking ($500–$1,200); fluid catch-up — engine oil, NSG370 manual trans fluid, transfer case, front/rear Dana 44 diff fluid (Tru-Lok compatible), brake fluid flush, coolant ($500–$900); return intake/exhaust to CARB-legal or OEM configuration for CA smog plus registration paperwork ($600–$1,500); reseal Freedom Top and door surrounds, pull carpet to dry/inspect floors; battery and door/tailg
profiles.repairs_12mo: Radiator and/or thermostat housing seep, water pump; front unit bearings if any hum or play; steering box if on-center play persists or wobble recurs; clutch hydraulic slave/clutch if pedal is heavy or engagement is high at 95k+; rear main / valve cover seep monitoring; shock and control-arm bushing replacement on the lift kit (MetalCloak joints are serviceable but wear); brake pads/rotors on the aftermarket big-brake kit — verify pad availability and cost before buying; sway bar disconnect motor/actuator; blend door actuator and window regulator; underbody rust arrest and cavity wax on any salt-belt truck; possible regear to 4.88 if running 35s and the truck feels overgeared ($1,800–$2,800).
profiles.market_notes: Rubicon and Rubicon X command a clear premium over Sahara/Sport, four-door Unlimited over two-door, and 2012+ Pentastar over the 3.8; the manual adds want-it factor with enthusiasts but narrows the buyer pool, and high-mileage manuals carry clutch risk that buyers discount. Documented, tastefully modified trucks with receipts and correct driveline/geometry work sell near clean-stock money; parts-catalog builds with no paperwork, mismatched lift components, or an unresolved wobble history sell well below. Desirable colors (Anvil, Gobi, Firecracker Red, Hydro Blue) and a Freedom Top plus soft top help; salt-belt provenance, rust on frame or control arm mounts, and non-CARB emissions hardware are hard price penalties in California. Mileage bands matter less than in normal cars — condition, rust, and records dominate — but sub-80k Rubicons still bring a premium, and anything over 120k is priced as a driver/build platform.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 90k-mile JK Rubicon typically needs a full deferred-fluid pass (manual trans, transfer case, both diffs, brake fluid, coolant), a fresh set of correctly sized tires, and a complete front-end refresh — lifted big-tire trucks eat ball joints, track bars and unit bearings on a 60k–100k cycle. Budget for the Pentastar oil filter housing and a radiator if not already documented, plus reseal work on the top and door surrounds. On any salt-belt example, add underbody rust arrest and cavity wax as a first-year project regardless of how it looks from ten feet.

profiles.label: Jeep Wrangler JL / Wrangler Unlimited JL (incl. Willys, 2018-present)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel buyer, a JL Willys is a fun, top-off coastal and Big Sur cruiser with real trail ability for Hollister Hills or occasional Sierra trips. It is a utility toy, not a commuter appliance. On-road manners depend almost entirely on how intact and well-maintained the front suspension and steering are. The 3.6 V6 with the 6-speed manual is the purist combination, but every 2018-2023 manual is subject to a clutch recall that must be verifiably closed. Because this buyer prefers unmodified cars, a lifted or 'off-road modified' JL needs install records and a careful front-end inspection, or it should be priced as a project.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Front-end 'death wobble' and wandering: the JL solid front axle is sensitive to a worn or under-damped steering damper, a loose or worn front track bar and its bushings, tie-rod and drag-link ends, ball joints, and incorrect caster after a lift. FCA issued revised steering dampers and several service bulletins for 2018-2021 trucks. Symptoms are violent shake after a bump at 45-60 mph, or a vague on-center feel. Fixes range from $300 (damper) to $800-1,500 (track bar, tie rod, drag link) to $2,000+ if a lift has to be corrected. Look for alignment sheets and records of the damper update.

2) Manual clutch pressure-plate recall: 2018-2023 JL and Gladiator 6-speed manuals were recalled because the pressure plate can overheat and fracture. The first remedy was a software update that adds a 'clutch hot' warning. A follow-up hardware remedy replaced the clutch and pressure plate. Require dealer proof that both are complete. Outside the recall, a clutch job runs $1,800-2,800. Also watch for clutch hydraulics (master/slave) issues: a soft or sinking pedal.

3) Pentastar 3.6 oil filter housing and oil cooler: the plastic assembly cracks or its gasket seeps oil and coolant into the valley. This is common from 40-80k miles and costs $500-900. Smell for hot oil and look down the back of the intake.

4) Pentastar water pump and thermostat housing seep. The water pump is timing-chain driven on the 3.6, so it is about $700-1,200. Check for pink crust at the front of the engine.

5) Steering gear box: leaks and free play develop, especially with larger tires. A box costs $900-1,600 installed. On 2018 trucks, also confirm the frame steering-gear-bracket weld recall.

6) Front axle wear: unit bearings ($350-600 per side), ball joints ($600-1,000), and axle-tube seals. Larger tires accelerate all of it. The rear Trac-Lok limited-slip needs the correct friction-modified fluid. Check for chatter in tight turns.

7) Lifts, larger tires, and wheel offset: these drive steering wear and incorrect speedometer readings. Tires of 35 inches or more on stock gears make the manual sluggish and hard on the clutch. A regear costs $2,500-3,500. Ask what parts were used and who installed them.

8) Water intrusion: Freedom Top panel seals, door seals, cowl, and windshield-frame seals leak, and the carpet holds water. Look for musty odor, damp foam, corrosion on under-seat connectors, and rust on floor pan bolts. Seals and adjustment cost $200-800.

9) Windshield cracks: common, and the JL windshield is expensive. Replacement is $600-1,500, more if a camera calibration is needed on optioned trucks.

10) Aluminum doors, hood, fenders, and tailgate: look for galvanic corrosion or bubbling where they meet steel hinges and fasteners. Also check for off-road dents to rock rails and skid plates.

11) Underbody trail damage: dented skid plates, a bent tie rod or drag link, scraped differential covers, a crushed muffler, and a dented gas tank skid. A Willys was marketed for trail use, so assume it was used that way.

12) Electrical and infotainment: Uconnect freezes or reboots, the backup camera drops out, and TPMS faults appear after wheel swaps. Automatic trucks with Engine Stop-Start add a small auxiliary battery that fails every 3-4 years ($150-300) and throws ESS or electrical warnings.

13) Transfer case and driveshafts: on the Command-Trac part-time case, check for a stiff or grinding 4H/4L shift and fluid leaks. Front driveshaft CV/U-joint wear accelerates on lifted trucks.

14) Coastal and salt exposure: Carmel fog plus any snow-country history matters. Inspect frame rails, crossmembers, brake lines, and exhaust hangers for scale. Check the title and Carfax history for Midwest or Northeast registration.

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Oil filter housing/cooler assembly replacement if seeping ($500-900).', 'Front end parts: tie rod ends, track bar bushings, ball joints as play develops ($400-1,500).', 'Front wheel hub/unit bearings if humming or showing play ($350-600 per side).', 'Tire replacement, often due on modified Jeeps with worn mud-terrains ($1,000-1,800 per set).', 'Main or auxiliary battery replacement ($150-350).', 'Coolant service and water pump if any weep appears ($700-1,200 if pump needed).', 'Windshield replacement if chipped or cracked ($600-1,500).', 'Undo or correct poorly done modifications (lift correction, steering correction, return to stock) ($500-3,000).']
profiles.market_notes: Price moves on body style (4-door Unlimited is the norm), trim (Rubicon > Sahara > Willys > Sport), and top (hardtop and Sky One-Touch command premiums over soft top). Mileage bands are under 30k, 30-60k, and over 60k. The 6-speed manual is rarer but trades flat to slightly below automatics in the broad market, so enthusiasts can buy it well. Modifications rarely add value and often subtract it for documented-stock buyers. A clean, stock, one-owner truck with dealer records and closed recalls is worth a meaningful premium. The ~$23k result on the example reflects high miles, mods, or condition questions more than strong demand.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 2022 is young but often trail-used. Expect a full driveline fluid service (diffs, transfer case, gearbox), an alignment, and a front-end bolt torque and inspection. Confirm the clutch recall is complete. On a modified truck, budget to correct or return to stock any poorly matched lift, steering, or tire setup before trusting it on Highway 1.

profiles.label: Lancia Delta HF Integrale Evoluzione II (Evo 2)
profiles.framing: This is the final, catalyzed 215hp development of the homologation-bred Integrale, and at current money it is a blue-chip Group A icon that the buyer intends to actually drive on Carmel Valley Road and Highway 1 — not park in a bubble. For this buyer the car must be a documented, unmolested, rust-free, numbers-correct Evo 2 with a legible ownership chain from Europe through import, because originality and provenance carry most of the value and almost all of the resale risk. Mechanically it is a hand-built Fiat-group turbo four with a demanding service clock: it rewards a fastidious owner and punishes deferred maintenance brutally. The decision hinges far more on rust, authenticity paperwork, and service history than on odometer reading.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural and cosmetic rust is the number one killer. Check the front strut towers and inner fender seams, the sills at the jacking points, the floor pans under the front carpets (water gets in past the plenum/scuttle drains and the windshield seal), the rear inner arches behind the boxed Evo fender flares, the tailgate lower edge and around the rear wiper motor, the sunroof drain channels if fitted, and the fuel filler bowl. Cars that lived in Northern Europe or spent winters in Italy are commonly patched. Proper metalwork plus a color-matched respray on a Blue Lagos car runs $8,000–30,000 and permanently dents value; look for old bodyshop invoices, paint-depth-gauge readings and photos of the car on a lift with the arch liners out.', 'Cambelt service is time-based, not mileage-based. The interval is roughly every 3 years or 36,000 km, and a snapped belt on this interference 16V head means bent valves and a $6,000–12,000 head rebuild. A 2020 belt on a 2026 car is out of date regardless of the 41,000 km on the clock. Demand a dated invoice covering belt, tensioner, water pump, and ideally the balance-shaft/auxiliary belt, from a shop that knows Lancias.', 'Head gasket failure and warped/cracked cylinder heads are classic Integrale problems, aggravated by overboost, poor coolant maintenance, and cars that sit. Symptoms: coolant loss with no external leak, pressurized expansion tank, mayonnaise under the cam cover, hot-idle misfire. Budget $4,000–8,000 for head off, skim, gasket, and valve work; a full bottom-end rebuild with pistons and rods is $18,000–30,000 at a specialist.', 'Turbo and boost control. The Garrett T3 (water-cooled) suffers shaft play and seal failure from hot shutdowns and stale oil; the wastegate actuator, boost solenoid and the vacuum/boost hose spaghetti perish and cause overboost cuts or soft running. Evo 2 cars also crack the cast exhaust manifold between runners. Turbo rebuild/replacement $2,000–4,500; manifold $1,200–2,500 with labor; hose renewal kit plus tuning $800–1,500.', 'Driveline: the Ferguson viscous center coupling degrades with age and low use, and a seized or dead VC gives tight-turn binding, driveline wind-up or vague traction; the Torsen rear diff can whine and its output seals leak. The five-speed transaxle is weak on second-gear synchro and suffers a notchy/obstructive shift from worn linkage bushings and a tired clutch hydraulic system. VC $2,000–3,500 installed, gearbox rebuild $4,500–8,000, clutch (dual-mass-free but labor-heavy) $1,800–3,000.', 'Cooling system and hot-running. Radiator, intercooler-to-throttle plumbing, the header/expansion tank and its cap, and the electric fan switch are all failure-prone; these cars run hot in traffic and a late fan is how heads get warped. Plan on a new radiator, hoses, thermostat, cap and fan relay as a matter of course — $1,500–2,500.', 'Bosch ABS system (ATE/Bosch hydraulic unit, accumulator and pump). A pulsing or permanently lit ABS light usually means a dead accumulator or pump motor; parts are scarce, and a rebuilt unit is $1,500–3,500. Test brake pedal feel and warning-light behavior cold and after a drive.', 'Electrics and grounds. Corroded earth points behind the battery tray and in the footwells cause phantom faults: dash warning lights, power window failure, erratic fuel gauge, fan and fuel-pump relay dropouts. The Marelli/Weber IAW ECU is generally robust but the crank sensor, air-temp sensor and injector harness insulation age out. Body ECU/relay board issues and the 5-digit odometer make mileage verification a documentation exercise, not an instrument-cluster one.', 'Interior trim is fragile and largely NLA. Dash tops crack, the Recaro bolsters and Crème leather on Blue Lagos cars stain and split, the center-dash oil pressure/temp gauge pod fades, headliners droop, and Evo-specific items (hood vents, adjustable rear spoiler, flare trim, Speedline Montecarlo center caps, correct Momo wheel) are expensive or unobtainable. Faded or

profiles.market_notes: Evo 2 sits at the top of the Integrale ladder, and within it the special editions — Blue Lagos, Giallo Ginestra, Bianco Perlato, Dealers Collection, Club HF Collection — carry a large premium over standard Rosso/Nero cars, with documented low-km, single-repaint-free examples now trading well into six figures. Provenance is price: a Lancia registry entry, original libretto/Fahrzeugbrief, matching engine and chassis numbers, an unbroken service file with dated cambelt invoices, and clean import paperwork can be worth 20–40% versus an undocumented car. Rust history, a respray, replaced Evo-specific trim, or a converted lesser Integrale destroy value disproportionately; conversely high-km but immaculate, heavily documented driver cars trade at a steep discount to museum-km cars and are often the better buy for someone who will actually use it. Manual is the only transmission; RHD conversions and non-original turbo/ECU tuning are discounts.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a 26k-mile Evo 2 is a 30-plus-year-old Italian turbo car whose rubber, fluids and fuel system have aged on the calendar rather than the odometer, so assume a full recommissioning: cambelt package, all coolant/vacuum/fuel hoses, tires, brake and clutch hydraulics, fluids, and battery/grounds. Low-mileage cars that sat are often worse than driven ones for seals, tank varnish, seized calipers and flat-spotted bushings. Budget roughly $6,000–10,000 of catch-up in the first year on a well-kept example, more if the A/C, ABS accumulator or viscous coupling need attention.

profiles.label: Land Rover Defender 110 (L663, 2020+)
profiles.framing: The L663 Defender 110 is an aluminum-monocoque luxury SUV with genuine off-road hardware. For a Carmel buyer it is a comfortable daily driver and weekend tool for Big Sur, the coast and trailheads. It is not a simple, owner-serviceable truck. Early 2020-2021 cars carry the most software, electrical and recall baggage, and most are now past the 4yr/50k factory warranty. Documented dealer software updates, recall completion, remaining CPO coverage, and a clean full-system scan matter more than cosmetics or mileage alone.
profiles.weak_points: ['Early-build electrical and software instability (2020-2021 especially). Symptoms include Pivi Pro screen freezes or reboots, a blank instrument cluster, intermittent key-fob and keyless-entry faults, and camera or parking-aid dropouts. Many cases were fixed by dealer or OTA software reflashes, but some needed module replacement. A head unit or cluster costs roughly $2,000-4,500 out of warranty. Look for dealer repair orders showing software updates and module replacements.', "12V and auxiliary battery drain. Early cars were notorious for flat batteries after sitting, which trigger cascading false warnings. Often cured by software plus new batteries. Main 12V battery $350-600, auxiliary battery $250-450 installed. Repeated battery replacements in the records point to an unresolved parasitic draw or module that won't sleep.", '48V mild-hybrid system (P400 inline-6 and later P300 MHEV). The belt-integrated starter-generator, 48V battery and DC-DC converter can fault. Symptoms are stop/start inoperative, charging warnings or no-start. Repair runs roughly $1,500-4,500 depending on component. A scan for 48V/BISG codes is essential.', 'Ingenium engine coolant leaks. The 3.0 inline-6 (P400) and 2.0 four-cylinder (P300) are known for seeping plastic coolant pipes, turbo coolant feed/return lines (superseded revised parts exist), and thermostat housing and auxiliary pump leaks. Symptoms are a sweet smell, a low-coolant message, and crusted residue around the turbo and rear of the head. Pipe repairs cost $400-1,800. Ignored leaks risk overheating and head or engine damage. Ask for the part number of any updated lines installed.', 'Ingenium engine and timing-chain risk. The chain is mounted at the rear of the engine, so chain or guide service is engine-out labor. Any engine replacement is roughly $18,000-30,000. The risk is low-frequency but real, and it rises with extended oil-change intervals, low oil level or poor-quality oil. Look for 7,500-10,000 mile or annual oil changes with correct-spec oil, not just the maximum-interval dealer schedule.', "Air suspension (standard on most US 110s). Air springs can leak (overnight sagging, uneven height), compressors wear out from overwork, and valve blocks and height sensors fail, bringing up a 'Suspension fault' or 'Reduced ride height' message. Costs are roughly $900-1,600 per air spring and $1,500-2,800 for a compressor at a dealer, less at an independent. Check that all height modes, access height and off-road height reach target and hold overnight.", 'Two-speed transfer case and differentials. Land Rover has issued transfer-case service and updates. Fluid neglect, or tire mismatch across axles, stresses the transfer case and center coupling. The optional active rear e-locker has actuator faults. A transfer case replacement is $4,000-7,000. Look for receipts for transfer-case, front and rear differential fluid changes, and any software update to the transfer case.', "ZF 8HP 8-speed automatic. The unit itself is robust, but it is marketed as 'lifetime fill.' A fluid and pan/filter service around 60-80k is prudent and costs $600-1,000. Harsh 2-3 shifts, flare or delayed engagement on a high-mileage car with no service record warrant caution.", 'Water ingress. Leaks show up at the side-hinged rear door seal, the sliding panoramic roof drains, the folding fabric roof (if fitted), and the Alpine roof lights. Symptoms are damp carpets, musty smells, fogged lamps and random electrical faults from wet connectors under the carpets or in the rear quarter. Fixes range from $200 for drain clearing to thousands if a module or harness is corroded.', "Rear door and exterior-mounted spare. The heavy side-hinged door carries the full-size spare, so check for door sag, a worn check strap, and misaligned latch or seal. Oversized aftermarket spares accelerate wear. Also inspect the aluminum body for galvanic corrosion where steel fasteners, the tow hitch or accessories contact aluminum. This matters more in C

profiles.market_notes: P400 inline-6 cars (SE, HSE, X, First Edition) bring more than P300 four-cylinder base and S cars. V8 and 130 models sit in a different price tier. Remaining transferable LR CPO coverage (7yr/100k from original in-service date) adds real money on 2020-2021 cars. So do documented recall and software completion and a clean Carfax, while prior LR 'buyback' or heavy repair history sharply discounts. Desirable options and packs include Off-Road Pack with e-locker, Towing Pack, Explorer or Adventure packs, the 3rd-row seat, and colors like Pangea Green, Gondwana Stone and Tasman Blue. Plain white or black cars with high miles (80k+) trade at a notable discount, and aftermarket lifts or tunes usually hurt resale to mainstream buyers.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2020-2021 example at 60-90k is past factory warranty and often has only dealer 'lifetime fluid' maintenance. Expect to catch up on the transfer case, differentials, transmission fluid, coolant, spark plugs and brake fluid ($1,500-3,000 total). Also verify all software and recall updates, and replace aging 12V/aux batteries. Budget for at least one coolant-leak fix and one air-suspension or electrical module repair within the first couple of years.

profiles.label: Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4 (L319, 2010–2016, incl. HSE Lux & Landmark)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LR4 is a genuinely capable, seven-seat family and Central Coast adventure wagon: Terrain Response, twin-speed transfer case, air suspension and real ground clearance in a package that still rides like a luxury car on Highway 1. It is not an investment and should never be bought as one — final-year 2016 Landmark cars have a modest collector halo, but running costs behave like a used luxury SUV with a hand-built British electrical system. What matters is documentation of the expensive stuff (timing chain hardware on the AJ126 supercharged V6, coolant pipes, air suspension, differentials) and a car that has been serviced by a specialist rather than deferred. Buy the best-documented example, not the cheapest, and budget a real reserve from day one.
profiles.weak_points:
1) AJ126 3.0 supercharged V6 timing chain and tensioner wear (2014–2016 cars, and the related AJ133 5.0 V8 chain issue on 2010–2013): a cold-start rattle of 1–3 seconds, chain stretch codes (P0016/P0017/P0018), or a whirring/ticking at idle points to guides and hydraulic tensioners. Failure is catastrophic (valve-to-piston contact). Preventive chain service is engine-out or front-cover-off labor, roughly $6,000–$10,000 at an independent, more at a dealer. Ask for a cold-start video with sound and any chain/tensioner invoices; unrecorded 90k+ cars carry this risk unpriced.
2) Plastic coolant crossover pipes / thermostat housing / water pump on the 3.0 SC: the OEM composite pipes under the supercharger go brittle with heat cycles and can split without warning, dumping coolant and risking overheat damage to an aluminum engine. Aftermarket billet-aluminum pipe upgrade kits exist and are the tell of a knowledgeable owner; expect $1,200–$2,500 done with the water pump and thermostat while access is open. Look for a receipt naming 'coolant crossover pipes,' 'aluminum pipe upgrade,' or supercharger removal.
3) Supercharger nose-cone bearings and the isolator/coupler: a whine changing pitch or a rattle at idle around 80–120k miles. Nose cone rebuild $600–$1,200; whole blower far more.
4) Air suspension: EAS compressor (Hitachi/AMK) and dryer wear out around 80–130k miles, symptoms are slow rise, 'Suspension Fault' messages, a car that sits low overnight, or a compressor that runs long and hot. Compressor with dryer $600–$1,400 installed; individual air springs $350–$700 each; valve block and height sensors add up. Coil-spring conversions are a red flag on a car this buyer wants unmodified.
5) Cooling-system periphery generally: expansion tank cracks, radiator and intercooler-circuit auxiliary pump, and the low-temp radiator on SC cars. A one-time overheat event can cook the engine — check for coolant staining in the vee and Carfax/dealer notes of 'overheating.'
6) Rear differential and driveshaft: rear diff bearing whine and pinion seal leaks appear from ~90k; center support bearing and rear driveshaft U-joints/flex disc cause a 40–60 mph vibration or clunk on throttle transitions. Driveshaft $700–$1,400, rear diff rebuild/replace $1,800–$3,500.
7) Front suspension wear items: lower control arm bushings and ball joints, plus front upper arms — typical at 70–110k, causing a shimmy over the mid-corner ruts on local backroads. All four arms $1,200–$2,000; alignment mandatory after air-suspension or arm work.
8) Sunroof and body drains: the triple-sunroof cars (Landmark, HSE Lux) plug drains and wet the headliner, A-pillars and, worse, the passenger footwell and front SRS/BCM connectors — check for damp carpet padding and musty smell. Also alpine window seals and tailgate/upper-glass hinge corrosion.
9) Electrical gremlins and parasitic drain: a weak battery causes cascading warning lights (park brake, suspension, transmission fault). Electric parking brake actuator module failure ($700–$1,200), HVAC blend-door actuators, front and rear camera/infotainment modules, and door-latch/window regulator faults are common. Always test every module cold and hot.
10) In-tank fuel pump / low-pressure fuel supply failures on the SC V6 (this generation has documented pump replacements around 60–90k, ~$900–$1,600) plus high-pressure pump and injector issues showing as long crank or misfire under load.
11) Oil leaks: cam cover gaskets, oil cooler/filter housing, and the timing cover on high-mile motors — usually $500–$1,500 each depending on access; a soaked engine bay masks the more serious coolant leaks.
12) Transmission: the ZF 8HP is strong but was 'filled for life.' A 98k car with no fluid service should get a pan/filter/fluid change ($500–$800); look for shudder at light throttle 1,200–1,600 rpm (torque converter lock-up) and harsh 2-3 shifts.
13) Brakes and tires: heavy vehicle, front rotors/pads every 30–40k ($900–$1,400 axle set with rotors); 20
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, ZF 8HP pan/filter/fluid if undocumented, front/rear diff and transfer case fluid, brake fluid, coolant condition test); four matching tires if the set is mixed or aged; new AGM battery unless dated within ~3 years; air-suspension full-cycle test and likely compressor/dryer service; clear all stored fault codes and re-scan after a 100-mile shakedown; clean all four sunroof and A-pillar drains; front brake pads/rotors if under 4mm; correct any cam-cover or oil-cooler seepage. Expect $2,500–$5,000 on a typical 90–100k example.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Coolant crossover pipe upgrade with water pump and thermostat if not already documented ($1,200–$2,500); front lower control arm bushings/ball joints and alignment ($1,200–$2,000); air spring(s) or valve block as leaks appear ($400–$1,500); supercharger nose-cone bearing or isolator if whining ($600–$1,200); rear driveshaft center bearing/flex disc or rear diff seals ($700–$1,800); HVAC actuator, parking-brake module or camera/infotainment module repair ($400–$1,200); spark plugs and both drive belts if not stamped. Timing-chain service is the big contingency if any cold-start rattle or chain codes appear.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by service documentation — a folder showing coolant pipes, chain hardware, air suspension and transmission service is worth several thousand dollars over an equal-mileage mystery car. Final-year 2016 cars, especially the Landmark and HSE Lux with three sunroofs, Meridian, surround cameras and the HD/heavy-duty package (full-size matching spare, locking rear diff), carry a premium; missing HD pack and mismatched 20" tires are cheapening details. Sub-80k-mile examples and desirable color combos (Santorini Black, Fuji White, Corris Grey over Ebony) bring the strongest money, while any Carfax damage entries, unrepaired suspension faults, or coil-spring conversions produce steep discounts. Regional bidding for these on BaT clusters $18k–$32k depending on miles and records, with hollow-market risk below $15k where the buyer inherits every deferred item.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 90–100k mile LR4 arrives with life-of-vehicle fluids never changed, an aging battery causing phantom faults, a tired air-suspension compressor and original coolant pipes. Plan on a comprehensive fluid and consumables catch-up plus air-suspension and cooling-system attention in the first year, and treat undocumented timing-chain hardware as an open $6k–$10k liability rather than a solved problem.
