profiles.label: Land Rover Range Rover Classic (US-market 1987–1995)
profiles.framing: For a Carmel-based buyer, a Range Rover Classic is a characterful, upright, genuinely capable 4x4 for coast and Carmel Valley use. It should be bought as an old British truck that needs ongoing care, not as a turnkey commuter. Condition matters most in two places: the steel structure hidden under the aluminum skins, and the health of the Rover V8's cooling system and head gaskets. Paint, interior and gadgets come a distant second. A documented, unmodified, rust-controlled example with a clean California smog history is worth a real premium over a cheaper truck that needs structural or engine work.
profiles.weak_points: ["Structural rust under aluminum panels. The outer skins are aluminum, but the inner structure and chassis are steel. Rust forms where the two metals meet and where water collects. Typical spots: the rear load floor and its supports, the inner and outer sills, the front footwells and bulkhead corners below the windscreen, the B/C-pillar bases, the lower tailgate frame and the upper tailgate glass frame. On the chassis, check the rear crossmember, the rear spring/shock towers, the outriggers and the radius-arm mounts. A fresh undercoat or 'rust inhibitor' spray can hide rot. Ask for pre-coating photos and probe the metal during inspection. Small patch work runs $1,500–4,000. Sill, floor or chassis rail repair runs $5,000–15,000 or more and can make a driver-grade truck uneconomic.", 'Rover 3.9L (and 4.2L LWB) V8 cooling and head gaskets. These alloy engines punish overheating. The usual failure chain is a clogged radiator, a weak viscous fan clutch, a failing water pump, or an air lock after amateur coolant work. The results are blown head gaskets or warped heads, and occasionally liner movement or cracked blocks. Warning signs: coolant loss with no visible leak, a pressurized overflow tank, mayonnaise on the oil cap, white exhaust smoke, or a temperature gauge that creeps on climbs. A head gasket job runs about $2,500–4,000. A rebuilt or exchange engine runs $8,000–15,000. Look for receipts covering the radiator, water pump, fan clutch, hoses and any previous head work.', 'Rover V8 lubrication and timing wear. The flat-tappet cam and lifters wear, especially on modern low-zinc oil, and show up as tapping lifters. The timing chain stretches and the cam gear wears; replacement runs about $800–1,500. The front cover and oil pump wear, causing low hot-idle oil pressure. Oil leaks are chronic at the rear main seal, the rocker covers, the timing cover and the oil cooler lines. Ask for oil-change intervals and the oil type used. At high mileage, budget for a leak-down test.', 'Lucas 14CUX fuel injection and ignition. Common faults: vacuum leaks from brittle hoses and the plenum gasket, failing hot-wire airflow meters ($300–700), idle stepper motor problems, and fuel pressure regulator faults. Also check for degraded in-tank fuel pump hoses, which cause stalling and are a fire risk; fuel pump work runs $400–900. Ignition faults come from the distributor cap, rotor, plug leads and amplifier. Symptoms are hunting idle, hesitation, hot-start problems and failed smog tests. Ask for fault code readouts and a smog report showing the HC, CO and NOx numbers.', "ZF 4HP22/4HP24 automatic transmission. These units are adequate but stressed by the truck's weight, towing, and fluid neglect. Watch for delayed engagement into Drive or Reverse, a slipping or flared 2–3 shift, harsh downshifts, and dark or burnt fluid. Cooler line leaks at the radiator are also common. A rebuild runs about $3,000–5,000 installed. Ask for fluid and filter service records. Heavy towing history, suggested by a receiver hitch, deserves extra scrutiny.", 'Transfer case and viscous coupling. US trucks from 1989 use the LT230 gear-drive transfer case with a viscous coupling in the center differential. Early 1987–88 trucks use the Borg-Warner chain-drive case. When the coupling seizes, the drivetrain binds on tight turns, scrubs tires and makes clunks. Mismatched tire sizes or tread depths accelerate this. A coupling replacement runs $700–1,500. Also check for output seal leaks, worn transfer case mounts, and the low-range shift. Do a tight-circle test on pavement.', 'Rover axles and swivel housings. Pitted chrome swivel balls tear their seals, leaking oil onto the brakes and letting grit into the CV joints. Other wear items are the swivel pin bearings, wheel bearings and pinion seals. A swivel rebuild runs $800–1,600 per side. Propshaft U-joints and the double-cardan front shaft are wear items at about $300–700 each. Look for oil-wet swivels and clunks on drive engagement.',
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter (high-zinc or flat-tappet-appropriate oil), ZF transmission fluid and filter, LT230 transfer case oil, front and rear differential oil, swivel housing oil or grease, power steering fluid', 'Cooling system refresh: flush, new thermostat, all rubber hoses, coolant reservoir cap, and inspection of the radiator, water pump and viscous fan clutch, with replacement as needed', 'Brake fluid flush with ABS accumulator and pump test, pads and rotors as needed, rubber brake hoses if original or cracked', 'Ignition and vacuum tune: distributor cap, rotor, plugs and leads, plus all vacuum and breather hoses, to stabilize idle and pass smog', 'Fuel system inspection: in-tank hoses, filter and pressure regulator; replace degraded fuel hoses immediately for fir
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Swivel ball and seal rebuild on one or both sides if leaking or pitted', 'Suspension bushing refresh: radius arms, Panhard rod, trailing links, plus shocks and the steering damper', 'Steering box reseal or adjustment if play or leaks are present', 'Propshaft U-joints and transfer case output seals', 'A/C system repair or proper R-134a conversion, including any evaporator, condenser, compressor or hose work', 'Exhaust manifold gaskets or studs and heat shield securing', 'Headliner re-cover and minor interior repairs (seat heaters, bolsters)', 'Electrical fixes: door lock actuators, window regulators, headlamp washer pump, gauge senders', 'Tailgate frame and localized rust repair before it progresses', 'Timing chain and gears, if high mileage with no record of replacement']
profiles.market_notes: Structural condition dominates price. A rust-controlled truck with a dry California or Southwest history and documented chassis, sills and tailgate commands a large premium over one with hidden rot. Late County LWB (1993–95, 4.2L, air suspension) and 1995 soft-dash County Classic trucks bring the most, followed by well-kept 3.9L County models, with desirable original colors such as Beluga Black, Alpine White, Portofino Red and Windsor Green helping. High-mileage driver-quality trucks with deferred A/C, cosmetic or rust issues trade roughly $10k–20k. Well-documented, sorted, unmodified examples bring $25k–45k, and restored or resto-mod trucks are a separate market well above that. Thick service files covering head gaskets, cooling, transmission and rust repair move price more than mileage. Aftermarket stereos, headlights and exhausts are mild negatives for originality-focused buyers.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most surviving trucks have 25–35 years of deferred rubber and fluids. Plan on replacing coolant and fuel hoses, bushings, brake hoses and seals, and on servicing every driveline fluid, before trusting the truck on longer drives. Also expect to address active corrosion at the steel/aluminum interfaces and to properly repair the A/C rather than recharge it, which typically adds $3,000–7,000 of catch-up work beyond the purchase price.

profiles.label: Lexus LX 470 (J100, 1998–2007)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LX 470 is the long-haul family/adventure truck: a 100-Series Land Cruiser with a bulletproof 2UZ-FE V8, full-time 4WD with a locking center diff, and enough leather and sound deadening to make Highway 1 and I-5 runs painless. Bought right, it is a 300k-mile vehicle; bought wrong, it is a rusty AHC-warning-light money pit with a $1,500 starter job hiding under the intake. What matters most here is a documented maintenance trail (timing belt/water pump, fluids, front axle service), a genuinely clean underbody, and an honest answer on the hydraulic suspension — either working and serviced, or converted with receipts and quality parts. Coastal Carmel salt air makes a rust-free California/Southwest history worth real money over a Northeast truck with a 'protected' frame.
profiles.weak_points: 1) AHC/TEMS hydraulic suspension is the defining risk. The nitrogen accumulators ('globes') lose charge by 100–150k miles, giving a harsh ride, slow raise/lower, and eventually an AHC warning light; globes run ~$150–250 each (four) plus labor, height control cylinders, the pump/accumulator assembly, and the height sensors add up fast — a full factory refresh is commonly $2,500–4,500. AHC fluid should be flushed every ~60k with Toyota AHC fluid; look for flush receipts and for the truck to cycle Low→N→High smoothly with pressure readings within spec (Techstream). Many trucks, like the example, have been 'AHC deleted' to conventional coils/shocks (OME, Dobinsons, Slee brackets) — that is an accepted and often preferable fix, but demand parts receipts, correct front spring rate, proper rear conversion hardware, and confirmation the dash lights/controls were addressed; a cheap delete with worn-out donor springs rides badly and sags. 2) Timing belt on the 2UZ-FE is due every 90k miles/9 years — always replaced with water pump, idler/tensioner bearings, thermostat, cam/crank seals and drive belts; $900–1,600 at an independent. A 2006 with a 2022/92k belt is on the clock by date, not miles, so budget it again around 2031 or sooner. 3) Starter is buried under the intake manifold: the part is ~$300 but labor makes it a $1,200–1,900 job; slow/clicking cranks or a hot-start hesitation means plan it, and do the intake-area hoses, PCV, and knock sensors while it is open. 4) Front axle service is the classic neglected item — birfield/CV joints, inner axle seals, knuckle wiper seals and wheel bearing repack; symptoms are grease slung on the inside of the wheels, gear-oil weeping from the knuckle, or a clicking on full-lock turns; a proper both-sides knuckle rebuild is $1,200–2,200. 5) Steering: power steering pump and high-pressure hose leaks, and on AHC trucks the pump also feeds the suspension, so a weeping pump is a two-system problem; sector shaft/box play and worn idler arm bushing cause the wandering 'Land Cruiser vagueness' — box, idler arm, and drag link/tie rod ends together are $1,000–2,000. 6) Suspension bushings and lower ball joints: original ball joints at 150k+ are a genuine safety item (use Toyota/555, not cheap aftermarket); upper/lower control arm bushings and sway bar bushings clunk from 120k. 7) Rust: rear frame section above the spring perches/rear crossmember, frame rails near the leaf-less coil mounts, rear quarter inner arches, hatch lower edge and tailgate seam, brake and fuel lines, and the rear bumper mounts — Northeast/Midwest trucks need the frame probed with a pick, not just photographed; a 'Woolwax/Fluid Film applied' note is good hygiene but can also mask scale. 8) Cooling and leaks: original radiator end tanks crack and the OEM radiator seeps at 120–180k ($500–800 installed); valve cover gaskets, oil cooler lines, front and rear main seals, and the oil pan (RTV, not gasket) commonly weep by 150k. 9) HVAC: rear heater lines corrode, blend-door/servo actuators fail causing one-side-cold, and the heater core is a dash-out job ($1,200–2,000); check both front and rear A/C blow cold and that the rear unit actually works. 10) Electronics: Mark Levinson amplifier and the 6-disc changer fail, the factory nav/display screen pixelates or goes dark, and the aging head unit is a $600–1,500 problem to solve properly (many owners fit a modern unit, which affects the 'unmodified' box but not the truck's integrity). 11) Interior wear items: sagging headliner, cracked dash top on sun-belt trucks, driver seat bolster and steering wheel leather wear, power antenna failures, and third-row latch/strap breakage; also door-lock actuators and the sliding-glass moonroof drains. 12) Driveline: rear driveshaft double-cardan and slip yoke wear causing vibration at 45–65 mph, propeller shaft flange bolt fretting (Toyota TSB), and differential/transfer case breather hoses; ATF (A343F on pre-'05, A750F on '05–'07) should have drain-and-fil
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid reset: engine oil, transfer case, front/rear differentials, transmission drain-and-fill, brake fluid, coolant if not pink/recent, and AHC fluid flush if still hydraulic. Replace the battery and terminals if age unknown, all four wipers, cabin/engine air filters, serpentine belt if undated. Expect a front-end refresh: lower ball joints, idler arm bushing, tie rod ends and an alignment if steering is vague ($800–1,600). Tires are commonly date-expired even with tread left — budget $1,000–1,400 for a set of 275/65R18 all-terrains. Fix any active AHC/VSC light, and address the usual minor leaks (valve covers, oil pan RTV weep) plus a rear main inspection. On a Northeast truck: dry-ice or needle-gun the frame, neutralize, prime, and re-cavity-wax before the first coastal winter ($800
profiles.repairs_12mo: Timing belt/water pump service if the current one is over ~7 years old regardless of mileage ($900–1,600). Starter replacement done proactively with intake off if cranking is at all lazy ($1,200–1,900). Front axle knuckle rebuild with birfields, inner seals and bearing repack if grease slinging or knuckle weeping ($1,200–2,200). Radiator and upper/lower hoses if original. AHC globes (all four) plus pump/height sensor attention if the truck is still hydraulic and rides harshly ($1,500–3,000), or a proper coil conversion with quality springs/shocks if going that route ($2,000–3,500 installed). Rear driveshaft double-cardan rebuild or replacement for highway vibration, control arm and sway bar bushings, blower/blend actuator work, headliner re-stretch, and a decent audio/nav solution if the M
profiles.market_notes: The 2003–2007 facelift trucks carry a clear premium, and 2005–2007 most of all for the VVT-i 4.7, 5-speed automatic, and updated interior/nav; a clean 2006 with sub-100k miles, two owners, and full records is the top of the market. Documented service (timing belt with water pump, AHC flushes or a receipted quality conversion, front axle service) moves price more than cosmetics, and a genuinely rust-free Western truck is worth $3,000–6,000 over an equivalent-mile salt-belt example. AHC that works and has been maintained appeals to purists; a well-executed delete is neutral-to-positive for most buyers and removes the biggest liability, while a broken AHC with lights on knocks thousands off. Third row, Mark Levinson, and locking center diff are expected on later trucks; conservative colors, tan/ivory interiors in good shape, and stock 18s help, while lifts, big tires, and bumpers narrow the buyer pool.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any J100 as 18–28 years old first and low-mileage second: rubber, hoses, belts, bushings, tires, and the AHC/power steering fluid circuits age out on the calendar even at 97k miles. A typical honest example needs $3,000–6,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year — fluids everywhere, front-end wear parts, a timing belt reset by date, cooling system refresh, and frame/underbody cleanup and cavity waxing if it spent time in the salt belt.

profiles.label: Lexus LX 570 (J200, 2008–2021)
profiles.framing: The J200 LX 570 is a Land Cruiser 200 with a luxury interior and hydraulic AHC/AVS suspension. For a Carmel buyer it is a long-lived, comfortable, capable daily driver and road-trip truck that can pass 300k miles if maintained. The 3UR-FE V8 and the transmission are rarely the problem. The expensive surprises come from the hydraulic systems (AHC suspension and the brake booster), secondary air injection on earlier trucks, and the lifts, wheels and overland builds many owners bolt on. Favor stock-height trucks with working, serviced AHC and real receipts over 'built' trucks priced as if the mods add value.
profiles.weak_points: ["AHC (Active Height Control) hydraulic suspension. The four wheel spheres ('globes'), the pump-side accumulator, the AHC shock/strut bodies, and the height sensors age out from roughly 100–150k miles or 12+ years. Symptoms include a harsh or bouncy ride, slow or uneven height changes, a flashing height indicator, sagging overnight, and wet shock bodies. Budget $1,500–2,800 for spheres plus accumulator at an independent shop, and $3,500–7,000+ for AHC shocks and a full refresh. A coil conversion (OME, Dobinsons and similar) costs $2,500–4,500 but is a modification. Ask for AHC fluid flush and sphere pressure-test receipts.", 'Lifted AHC trucks. These are raised with height-sensor link adjusters, torsion-bar re-indexing, or spacers, as in the example listing. The lift changes CV and upper-control-arm angles and alignment, and it confuses headlight leveling. It accelerates CV boot tears, ball joint wear and inner axle wear. Ask for the lift receipt, the exact method used, and a post-lift alignment printout. Returning a truck to stock costs about $300–1,500 depending on method.', 'Secondary Air Injection (SAI) pumps and switching valves on 3UR-FE trucks, mainly 2008 to early-2010s. Water intrusion and carbon cause the pump or valves to fail, setting P2440, P2442, P2444, P0418 and related codes. The truck may go into limp mode and will fail California smog. Expect $1,200–3,500 depending on whether one or both valves plus the pump are replaced. Some years had extended Toyota coverage, now long expired. Ask for replacement records or a clean scan with SAI readiness complete.', 'Hydraulic brake booster pump and accumulator (not a vacuum booster). Symptoms are the pump running or buzzing excessively, brake/ABS/VSC warning lights, and a hard pedal after sitting. The pump-and-motor assembly or accumulator costs about $1,500–3,000 installed. Brake fluid must be replaced on schedule; old fluid shortens booster life.', '3UR-FE water pump and thermostat. Weeping at the pump weep hole leaves pink or white crust on the timing cover and a slow coolant loss, typically 90–150k miles. Replacement runs $700–1,500 with the thermostat and Toyota SLLC coolant. Ask for water pump receipts on any truck past about 120k.', 'Cam tower, timing cover and valve cover seepage on the 3UR-FE. A slow oil seep at the cam tower seams, with oil on the heads or a burning smell, is common with age. A cam tower reseal is a $1,500–3,000 labor-heavy job; valve cover gaskets run about $500–900. Seepage is usually monitor-only unless oil is dripping onto the exhaust.', 'Radiator and cooling system aging. The plastic tanks crack, and the radiator carries an integrated transmission cooler circuit. Budget $700–1,400 for a radiator, hoses and a coolant service. An overheating event on a heavy V8 truck is a deal-breaker without records.', "Transmission service neglect. Toyota calls the fluid 'lifetime' (6-speed AB60E 2008–2015; 8-speed AA80E 2016–2021). Neglect shows up as harsh 2–3 or 3–4 shifts, torque converter shudder at 40–50 mph, and a delayed engagement into gear. A drain-and-fill with WS fluid every 60k costs $200–400. A rebuild or replacement is $4,000–7,000. Rare, but towing history matters.", 'Front suspension wear. Upper control arm bushings and ball joints, lower ball joints, tie rod ends, and front wheel hub bearings wear out on these 6,000-lb trucks, especially on oversize all-terrain tires. Expect clunks over bumps, humming at speed, and uneven tire wear. Control arms cost $600–1,200 per pair installed; hub bearings run $400–800 per side.', 'Front CV axles and boots, plus front differential and transfer case seals. Look for torn boots slinging grease, clicking on full lock, and weeping pinion or axle seals. Lifted trucks are much worse. CV axles run $300–700 per side; seals run $250–600 each.', 'Spark plugs and ignition coils. Plugs are on a 120k interval and are labor-heavy on the V8. A misfire over 150k often means the original plugs were never done. Plugs co

profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Water pump and thermostat if the original pump is past about 120k', 'AHC spheres and accumulator, or AHC shock replacement, if the ride is harsh or pressure tests are low', 'Front brake pads and rotors, plus rear pads', 'Upper control arms, ball joints and tie rod ends', 'Front wheel hub bearings', 'Valve cover gaskets or cam tower seep repair if it becomes an active leak', 'SAI pump or valves on earlier trucks if codes appear', 'Radiator and coolant hoses if the tanks are discolored or weeping', 'Front CV axle or boot replacement', 'A/C service or rear A/C line repair if cooling is weak', 'Seat heater or ventilation element and bolster repair']
profiles.market_notes: The 2016–2021 facelift (8-speed, updated interior and safety tech) commands a large premium over 2013–2015 spindle-grille trucks, which in turn sell above the cheapest 2008–2012 examples. Under 150k miles with dealer or specialist records sells at a premium. Trucks at 180k+ trade at a steep discount even though the drivetrain can go much further, which makes documented high-mile trucks the value play. Verified AHC health and SAI records move price meaningfully. Lifts, aftermarket wheels, racks and sliders are often priced up by sellers but should be discounted by a stock-preferring buyer. Clean black, white pearl and dark gray colors, Luxury or rear-entertainment packages, and the 2019–2021 Inspiration or Sport trims help resale.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 12–16-year-old, 150k+ LX 570 needs a fluids reset (transmission, diffs, transfer case, AHC, brake, coolant), plugs, and a water pump if these are undocumented. Expect roughly $2,000–4,000 in catch-up before addressing AHC or brake booster health. Lifted or overland-built examples usually add alignment, CV and suspension-joint work, or a return to stock height.

profiles.label: Lexus LX450 (80-Series / FZJ80, 1996–1997)
profiles.framing: The LX450 is a Lexus-trimmed 80-Series Land Cruiser with the 1FZ-FE 4.5L inline-six, A442F four-speed automatic, and full-time 4WD with a center diff lock. US LX450s were not offered with the factory front and rear lockers available on the Land Cruiser. For a Carmel driver it makes sense as a durable, comfortable utility truck for Highway 1, Big Sur, beach access, and Sierra snow trips, as long as the buyer accepts roughly 12–14 mpg and 1990s braking. The money is in documented cooling, head gasket, and front axle work, a rust-free body, and a stock or reversibly modified chassis that still passes a California smog check. Heavily built overland trucks like the example listing need extra scrutiny for lift geometry and emissions legality, and the accident history, refinished panels, and recent in-frame rebuild all need verification.
profiles.weak_points: ['Head gasket (1FZ-FE): Most common at 200k+ miles or after any overheating. The rear of the head near the firewall is the usual failure area. Symptoms are slow coolant loss with no visible leak, white exhaust smoke, combustion gas in the coolant, and an overheat on long grades or when towing. An independent shop charges roughly $3,000–5,000 in California, including head machining, valve job, and gaskets. Ask for receipts naming the machine shop and the head bolt torque procedure. A truck with a documented head gasket job done with OEM gaskets is worth a premium.', 'Cooling system: The original-style radiators have plastic tanks that crack. The firewall heater control valve is a notorious leak point, and the fan clutch and water pump weep with age. Budget $600–1,500 for radiator, hoses, fan clutch, and thermostat. A 1FZ that has run hot is a head gasket candidate, so look for receipts with dates and brand names. OEM or Koyo/Denso parts are preferred.', 'Rear heater and rear A/C lines: These steel and rubber lines run under the body to the rear heater and A/C. They rot or chafe and dump coolant or refrigerant without obvious warning. Many trucks have the rear heater bypassed. A bypass is acceptable, but it should be disclosed. Repair runs $300–800. Ask whether the lines were replaced or bypassed, and inspect them on a lift.', 'Front axle knuckles and Birfield joints: Expect trunnion (knuckle) bearings, wheel bearings, and wiper seals to need a full rebuild every 100–150k miles. Signs are grease or gear oil weeping from the knuckle ball, play in the knuckle, front-end shimmy, and Birfield (CV) clicking on tight turns. A full front axle service runs roughly $1,800–3,500 for both sides, more if Birfields or spindles are needed. This is one of the most important records to find.', 'Steering box, pump, and hoses: Leaks from the steering box sector shaft seal and the pump are common, along with excess on-center play. A worn box combined with worn tie rods, drag link, and steering damper produces vague tracking and shimmy. Hoses cost $200–500. A rebuilt box installed runs about $800–1,500.', "Driveshafts and the '80-series clunk': A dry front or rear driveshaft slip yoke causes a clunk on takeoff or when shifting into gear, and worn U-joints vibrate. The fix is often just grease every 3–5k miles, but a truck that clunks with no grease history may also have worn U-joints or a worn double-cardan joint, roughly $300–900 per shaft.", 'A442F transmission and HF2A transfer case: Both are robust but not immortal past 250k miles, especially after towing, lifts with bigger tires, or neglected fluid. Watch for delayed engagement, a soft or flaring 3–4 shift, shudder, or burnt-smelling fluid. A rebuild runs about $3,500–5,500. The center diff lock vacuum actuator and indicator can stick or fail to engage or release, typically $300–800 to repair. Ask for fluid change intervals.', 'Starter solenoid contacts: The starter is buried under the intake manifold, and its solenoid contacts wear out. The symptom is a single click and no crank, often intermittent and worse when hot. The contacts kit is cheap, but labor is $800–1,500 as a standalone job because the intake must come off. A smart owner does it alongside a head gasket job, so ask whether it was.', 'Valve adjustment and ignition: The 1FZ-FE uses shim-under-bucket valves due for adjustment about every 60k miles, and it is often skipped. Tight valves lead to burnt valves and rough idle. An adjustment runs about $600–1,000. Distributor cap and rotor, plug wires, and the distributor O-ring (an oil leak) are routine wear items.', 'Oil leaks and exhaust manifold: Valve cover gasket, oil filter housing and oil cooler lines, front crank seal, and rear main seal leaks are common, as is oil pan seepage. The cast exhaust manifold can crack and its studs break, producing a ticking noise on cold start; repair runs $800–1,800. Note that the factory oil pressure gauge and sender are notoriously erratic. Verify
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil, ATF, transfer case, front and rear differentials, Toyota Red coolant flush, power steering, and brake fluid flush', 'Grease all driveshaft slip yokes, U-joints, and front knuckle zerks; inspect for clunk and play', 'Cooling system pressure test and combustion leak (block) test; replace the heater control valve and any cracked hoses', 'Inspect, and if necessary replace or bypass, the rear heater and A/C lines under the body', 'Tune-up if undocumented: plugs, distributor cap and rotor, wires, air and fuel filters', 'Valve adjustment if no record within the last 60k miles', 'Tire age and condition, alignment with caster check (critical on lifted trucks), and brake pad and rotor inspection', 'California smog check, VIN verification, and title transfer for out
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front axle knuckle service (trunnion bearings, wheel bearings, seals, Birfield inspection) if not documented within ~100k miles', 'Steering box reseal or replacement, power steering pump, and tie rod, drag link, and damper refresh', 'Suspension bushing refresh (radius arms, trailing arms, panhard) and shocks; coils if sagging', 'Starter solenoid contacts, ideally combined with any intake-off work', 'Valve cover gasket, oil cooler line, and distributor O-ring leak repairs', 'Exhaust manifold stud or crack repair if ticking is present', 'A/C service; possible compressor, expansion valve, or rear A/C repair', 'Rear axle full-floater hub service and axle seals', 'Rust treatment and undercoating appropriate to coastal Carmel conditions']
profiles.market_notes: LX450s generally trade at or slightly below equivalent Land Cruisers because they lack factory lockers, though clean, stock, low-mileage examples now command strong prices. Price is driven by documented head gasket, cooling, and front axle work, a rust-free Western or Southern history, and an unmodified or tastefully modified chassis. Clean-Carfax trucks under ~150k miles bring a large premium over 200k+ trucks. Heavily built overland trucks sell to a different buyer pool, and an accident history, refinished panels, or a recent in-frame rebuild without strong receipts should discount meaningfully.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 25+ year-old LX450 needs a cooling system refresh, a full fluid baseline, front axle knuckle service, steering and suspension bushing work, and attention to rear heater lines and sunroof drains. Plan $3,000–6,000 of catch-up even on a good truck. Trucks with an undocumented head gasket or a warm-running history should be priced as if a head gasket job is coming.

profiles.label: Lexus RX 350 (AL10, 3rd generation)
profiles.framing: This is the low-drama family/utility slot in the garage: a 2GR-powered, port-or-D4S V6 crossover with a properly engineered automatic, a quiet cabin, and a parts and service network that reaches everywhere. For a Carmel-based buyer it is a Highway 1 / Salinas run-around and airport hauler that should never be the reason a weekend gets cancelled. Nothing about it is engaging, so the entire buying case rests on documentation, condition, and price relative to a market that stubbornly refuses to depreciate. Note that US-market 2010–2015 cars are the true AL10 with the 2GR-FE and U660E/U760E; 2016 is the AL20 redesign with the 2GR-FKS and 8-speed — mechanically similar in spirit but a different platform, so verify which car you are actually looking at.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing-cover and cam-tower oil seepage on the 2GR-FE is the signature 100k+ issue: the RTV-sealed front cover weeps down the back of the block and onto the subframe, often mistaken for a rear main leak. Diagnosis is easy from below with a light; repair is engine-out-of-the-way labor at roughly $1,800–3,000 at an independent. Ask for photos of a clean underside or a documented reseal. 2) Water pump failure/weeping around 80k–130k, usually announced by pink crust at the weep hole or a faint coolant smell; $500–900 including the belt. 3) The VVT-i oil supply line failure that killed early 2GR engines was addressed by recall/updated hard line on earlier cars, but on any 2GR verify the metal line is present and dry — a burst line dumps oil in seconds and destroys the engine. 4) U660E/U760E 6-speed: Lexus calls the WS fluid 'lifetime,' which it is not. Neglected units develop a 1-2 shift flare, torque-converter shudder at light throttle 35–50 mph, or a delayed engagement clunk. Drain-and-fills every 60k are cheap insurance; a car at 120k with zero fluid history is a $3,500–5,000 gamble. 2013+ F Sport uses the 8-speed U880E, which is fine but has its own valve-body software updates. 5) Melting/sticky and cracking dashboards on 2010–2013 cars, especially sun-belt and coastal-sun examples — Lexus ran a warranty extension that has now expired; replacement is $1,400–2,500. Check the top pad and the passenger airbag seam. 6) HVAC blend-door and mode actuators tick or knock behind the dash and cause split hot/cold; $250–600 each depending on access. 7) Remote Touch mouse controller and the 8-inch nav screen: sticky/erratic cursor, ghost touches, screen delamination or DVD/HDD nav drive failure. New OEM units are $900–1,800; many owners live with it or fit an aftermarket head unit (a modification this buyer should be wary of, as it often means hacked wiring). 8) Power liftgate struts and the electric lift actuator/motor fail around 100k — the gate drops, beeps, or refuses to latch; struts are cheap, the actuator is $600–1,000. 9) Suspension: front lower control arm bushings, sway bar end links, and strut mounts produce a clunk over Carmel Valley pavement joints by 100k–120k; struts and mounts all around run $1,200–2,000. Rear wheel bearings hum from ~120k, $400–600 each. 10) Hydraulic engine and transmission mounts collapse and cause a diesel-like idle shake in Drive; front mount $350–650 installed. 11) Spark plugs are a 120k service and the rear bank requires intake plenum removal — budget $450–700, not $120. 12) A/C condenser stone damage and slow leaks are common on freeway cars; condenser plus recharge $700–1,100. Also check for the compressor clutch rattle at idle. 13) AWD models: the transfer case and rear diff fluids are almost never changed, and the driveshaft center support bearing rumbles at 40–60 mph on higher-mileage cars. 14) Sunroof drains clog with coastal pine needles and Monterey litter, soaking the A-pillar trim and headliner — pull the trim and look for water staining, plus check the spare well for standing water.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: transmission WS drain-and-fill (repeat in 500 miles if the old fluid is dark), coolant if past 10 years, brake fluid flush, transfer case and rear diff on AWD. Four new tires if the DOT codes are over six years old regardless of tread (very common on low-mile Lexus SUVs), plus an alignment. New 12V battery if undated or over four years, cabin and engine air filters, wiper blades, and a sunroof-drain flush. Expect to fix at least one HVAC actuator tick or a pair of liftgate struts. Budget $1,500–2,800.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not documented; timing-cover reseal if seepage is dripping rather than weeping; spark plugs and coil inspection at 120k; front strut assemblies and sway bar links if it clunks; engine and transmission mounts if it shakes at idle in Drive; a rear wheel bearing; brake pads and rotors all around; possibly a dash pad replacement on a 2010–2013 sun-baked car. Budget $2,000–4,000.
profiles.market_notes: RX 350s trade on records and mileage bands more than on spec — a one-owner car with a full Lexus dealer history and under 90k will command a real premium over an identical 120k trade-in. AWD carries a modest premium nationally but matters little on the Monterey Peninsula, so FWD is the value play; Navigation/Premium/Luxury packages, ventilated seats, blind-spot monitor, and the 2013+ F Sport add appeal, while the F Sport's stiffer ride and 19s add nothing for this mission. Neutral colors (Nebula Gray, Starfire Pearl, silver) with tan or black leather sell fastest; a clean, unmodified California car with no rust, no accidents, and a factory head unit is worth paying up for because the whole point of this vehicle is not thinking about it.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-15 year old RX arrives with 'lifetime' fluids that were never changed, original coolant, aging suspension bushings, and six-to-eight-year-old tires on a low-mile example. Plan on a full fluids-and-rubber reset in the first month — trans, coolant, brake fluid, diff/transfer case, tires, battery, belt — then treat water pump, spark plugs, and struts as scheduled 12-month items rather than surprises.

profiles.label: Lexus RX350 (XU30, 2007–2009)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the XU30 RX350 is a quiet, comfortable, low-drama daily and road-trip vehicle for Highway 1, foggy wet coastal winters, and the occasional Sierra run. The 2GR-FE V6 and U151E five-speed can easily pass 200k miles when fluids have been changed, so the purchase decision rests on documented maintenance and on the cost of predictable age items: dash, steering rack, suspension bushings, headlights, and electronics. AWD is useful but not essential on the coast. A clean FWD car with records beats a neglected AWD one. Treat every listed 'cosmetic' flaw as a line item with a price.
profiles.weak_points: ["VVT-i oil cooler line (2GR-FE): early 2GR engines used a line with a rubber hose section feeding the intake cam phasers. It can split suddenly, dump the engine oil in seconds, and destroy the engine. Lexus ran a limited service campaign to replace it with an all-metal line. Look for a dealer campaign record, or a photo or inspection confirming the all-metal line on the right/rear of the engine near the timing cover. If it hasn't been done, the parts and labor are a few hundred dollars. Skipping it risks a $5,000–8,000+ engine replacement. This is the single most important item on the car.", 'Power steering rack and hoses: rack seal leaks, typically from 80–150k miles or 12+ years, show up as wet boots, ATF-type fluid on the subframe, groaning at full lock, or a dropping reservoir level. A replacement rack costs roughly $1,200–2,200 installed. The pressure and return hoses also weep. A recently replaced rack with a receipt is a real positive.', "Dashboard cracking: the 2004–2009 RX dash pad cracks and shrinks from UV and heat, usually starting near the defrost vents and passenger airbag seam. Lexus's dashboard extended-coverage program has largely expired. A full dash replacement runs about $1,500–2,500 at an independent shop. The alternatives are a molded overlay cover or a filler kit. An airbag-area crack can matter for inspection and resale.", 'Water pump (2GR-FE, belt-driven): weep-hole seepage and pink or white coolant crust on the pump body are common at 80–130k miles or with age. Replacement runs about $500–900, with a coolant service at the same time. Look for records of Toyota/Lexus SLLC pink coolant. The first service is due at 100k miles or 10 years, then every 50k miles or 5 years.', "U151E five-speed automatic: Toyota called the WS fluid 'lifetime', so many cars have never had it changed. Symptoms are harsh 2–3 or 3–4 shifts, flare on upshift, delayed engagement into Drive/Reverse, and torque converter shudder at light throttle around 40–50 mph. Preferred maintenance is repeated drain-and-fills with Toyota WS fluid. A machine 'flush' on a high-mileage neglected unit can sometimes trigger problems. Valve body or solenoid work costs about $800–1,500. A reman transmission costs about $3,500–5,000.", 'AWD driveline (AWD models): the transfer/PTU and rear differential use gear oil that is often never changed. PTU output seal and vent leaks are common. Neglected PTUs can overheat, whine, or bind, and rebuild or replacement runs about $1,500–3,000. Also check the propeller shaft center support bearing, the rear diff mount bushings, and the CV boots. Ask for records of transfer and rear diff fluid changes.', 'Front suspension: the front lower control arm bushings (especially the rear horizontal bushing) crack and cause clunks, wandering, and uneven tire wear. Sway bar links and strut mounts also wear. Arms with bushings and ball joints cost about $500–1,000 per pair installed. Struts and mounts cost about $800–1,500 per axle pair if they are original and soft. An alignment is needed afterward.', 'Air suspension (Height Control / Adaptive Variable Suspension, optional on Premium-equipped cars): air springs crack with age, and the compressor or height sensors fail. Symptoms are sagging overnight, a height-control warning light, or the compressor running constantly. Expect about $400–800 per air spring and $800–1,500 for a compressor. Coil conversion kits count as a modification. Verify which suspension the car has and test raising and lowering it.', 'Headlights with AFS: the swiveling Adaptive Front Lighting System motors and sensors fail, flashing the AFS light at startup. Housings fog or take on moisture as seals age. HID ballasts and igniters can fail at $200–500 each. A new OE headlamp assembly can cost $800–1,500+ each. Moisture inside the housing usually means seal failure, not a simple fix.', 'Navigation, display, and backup camera: the touchscreen can develop dead zones, the display can dim or fail, and the backup

Replace it immediately if it is the original rubber-section line.', 'Engine oil and filter (0W-20), engine air filter, and cabin air filter.', 'Brake fluid flush. Rear pads and rotors with caliper slide-pin service if the rear pads are low or wearing unevenly.', 'ATF drain-and-fill with Toyota WS if there is no record within about 30k miles or 3 years. profiles.market_notes: The RX350 (2GR-FE, 2007–2009) brings more than the earlier RX330. Low miles (under 80k), one-family ownership, a window sticker, and continuous service records produce the strongest results, especially on enthusiast auction sites. AWD, Premium Plus, Navigation, Mark Levinson, and the 2008–2009 Pebble Beach Edition add value. A badly cracked dash, failed air suspension, foggy headlights, or electronics faults are used to negotiate down roughly by their repair cost. Neutral colors (white, silver, black, smoky granite) with ivory or black leather are the norm. Clean, documented, low-mile examples generally trade high-single-digit to mid-teens thousands, while high-mile cars with no records sell well below that.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2007–2009 RX350 is 15+ years old, and rubber has aged regardless of mileage. Expect catch-up on all fluids (ATF, transfer/diff, coolant, brake), tires by date code, suspension bushings, and possibly PS hoses and the water pump. Budget roughly $1,500–3,500 for this catch-up on a documented car. Add more for dash, headlights, or air suspension if those are faulty.

profiles.label: MINI Cooper S John Cooper Works GP (R53 GP1, 2006)
profiles.framing: The GP1 is the most focused R53: a two-seat, Bertone-finished, factory-JCW-tuned supercharged hatch with a mechanical LSD, stiffer and lower suspension, and unique wheels and aero. For a Carmel driver it suits Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road, and Laureles Grade, and Tritec/R53 running gear is cheap and well understood. GP-only pieces are scarce, though, and a 20-year-old example lives or dies on the supercharger, gearbox, power-steering pump, rubber, and rust history. A documented, unmodified, accident-light car is worth paying up for. A tired, modified, salt-state car is a parts-hunting project dressed up as a bargain.
profiles.weak_points: ["Supercharger (Eaton M45, JCW-spec on the GP): the sealed nose oil is effectively a wear item. Without service, bearings and coupler wear between roughly 60k and 100k miles. Symptoms are a louder or rattly whine at idle, a 'marbles' rattle that changes when the clutch is pressed, and lost boost. An oil service is cheap. A rebuild or exchange unit runs about $600–$1,500 installed. Ask for a dated rebuild invoice that names the shop or rebuilder and the parts replaced, not just 'rebuilt.' Aftermarket reduction pulleys add boost and speed up supercharger wear.", 'Crankshaft harmonic damper (crank pulley): the factory rubber-bonded damper delaminates with age. The outer ring wobbles or walks off, which leads to belt shredding, vibration, and possible damage to the crank snout or timing cover. This is a must-check on any example over about 10 years or 80k miles. An OEM or ATI replacement plus labor runs about $350–$900. Record the part brand and date, and note that an ATI damper usually comes paired with a reduction pulley.', 'Electro-hydraulic power steering (EHPS) pump: the pump sits low behind the front bumper, and its small cooling fan fails or clogs. The pump then overheats, and steering goes heavy or intermittent, often after hot or slow driving. A failed pump costs about $800–$1,600 for a reman unit installed. A preventive fan replacement or retrofit is about $100–$250. Look for receipts for the fan or pump, and inspect for fluid leaks and a crusty, corroded harness at the pump.', "Getrag 6-speed gearbox with mechanical LSD: R53 boxes are known for input and output shaft bearing whine, which is worst on overrun or at steady cruise and changes with load. Expect occasional 2nd/3rd synchro crunch on high-mileage or hard-driven cars. A rebuild or used replacement runs about $2,500–$5,000, and a correct LSD-equipped unit costs more and is harder to find. This is a manual with no serviceable filter, so a 'transmission filter replaced' claim points to sloppy records.", "Clutch and flywheel: the GP's extra torque plus enthusiast use wears clutches. Many R53s also get single-mass flywheel conversions, which add chatter and gear rattle. Check for slip in 4th–5th at low rpm under full load, a high engagement point, judder, and slave cylinder or hose leaks. A clutch with a flywheel runs about $1,300–$2,800. Ask for the clutch replacement mileage and the brand of clutch and flywheel.", "Cooling system plastics: the water pump has a plastic impeller, and the plastic thermostat housing, coolant expansion tank, and hoses all crack or weep with age. Overheating on the Tritec risks the head gasket and warping. A water pump, thermostat housing, and tank refresh runs about $500–$1,000. The radiator fan and its resistor or control module also fail, which shows up as rising temps in traffic; budget about $250–$600 for that. Look for coolant crust at the housing on the driver's side of the head and under the reservoir.", 'Tritec oil leaks: common sources are the oil filter housing gasket, valve cover gasket, oil pan gasket, rear main seal, and supercharger and manifold gaskets. Leaking oil fouls belts and soaks engine mounts. Typical leak repairs run $200–$800 each, and a rear main seal is best done alongside a clutch job. Wet undersides plus fresh gasket receipts can mean either a sorted car or one still chasing leaks.', "Engine and transmission mounts: the upper passenger-side hydromount and the lower 'dog bone' torque arm mount wear. Symptoms are clunks on throttle tip-in and lift, excessive engine rock, and vibration at idle. Expect about $300–$800 for a full set. Stiffer aftermarket mounts add cabin vibration.", 'Front control arm rear (thrust) bushings, strut mounts, and sway bar links: these produce clunks, vague turn-in, steering wheel shimmy under braking, and uneven tire wear. Arms or Powerflex-type bushings plus an alignment run about $400–$1,000. Adjustable or aftermarket arms should come with a recent alignment sheet.', 'Rear subfram
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid baseline: engine oil and filter, coolant flush with correct BMW/MINI coolant, brake fluid flush, and manual transmission fluid change using MINI-approved MTF. Add a supercharger oil service if there is no record within about 50k miles.', 'Inspect the crank harmonic damper for rubber cracking or ring wobble, and replace it if it is original or undocumented. Replace the serpentine belt and tensioner if they are aged or noisy.', 'Check the EHPS pump cooling fan and clean the pump area. Replace or retrofit the fan preventively if it is original.', 'Replace worn engine mounts, particularly the upper passenger-side mount and the lower dog bone, if there is clunking or excessive rock.', 'Tires: replace any tires over 6 years old or mismatched. Decide on run-flats versus non-run-flats
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front control arm rear bushings, sway bar links and bushings, and strut mounts as clunks develop.', 'Rear trailing arm bushings and a rear suspension squeak diagnosis (shocks, mounts, and bushings).', 'Reseal the oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets if not recently done. Investigate pan and rear main seal leaks.', 'Preventive water pump and thermostat housing replacement if not documented in the last 5 years or 60k miles. Check the radiator fan and its resistor or control module.', 'Window regulator replacement as cables fail. Headliner re-cover if sagging (about $300–$600).', 'Brake service: pads, rotors, and a check of caliper slide and seal condition. Replace any aged rubber brake hoses.', 'Clutch replacement if engagement is high, slip appears, or the clutch is undocumented pas
profiles.market_notes: Only about 415 GP1s were sold in the U.S., and all came in Thunder Blue Metallic with a silver roof and red mirrors, so color does not move price. Condition, originality, mileage, and history do. Unmodified examples command the strongest prices, especially those with intact original suspension, unbent GP wheels, the carbon wing, aero, Recaros, the rear brace, the numbered plaque, the window sticker, and continuous records. Low-mileage clean-Carfax cars bring clear premiums. High-mileage (100k+), modified, accident-reported, or salt-state cars with rust or a replaced subframe trade at a steep discount. Some of these sell for well under typical GP values, but they often need $3k–$8k of sorting, and their originality may be hard to recover.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2006 GP needs a 20-year rubber-and-plastics catch-up: the crank damper, engine mounts, suspension bushings, coolant plastics, belts, and hoses, plus supercharger oil and gearbox fluid if undocumented. Budget roughly $2,000–$5,000 beyond purchase for a 'running and driving' example to make it reliable. Cars from salt states should also get an underbody rust reckoning before any money goes into refinement.

profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (NA, 1990–1997)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the NA Miata is a cheap-to-own, top-down Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road car — a 2,200-lb, 116–133 hp roadster whose whole appeal is steering feel, shifter quality and the ability to drive it hard at legal-ish speeds. It is not a hauler and not an investment; the right car is a rust-free, documented, largely stock West Coast example where the timing belt, cooling system and soft top are already sorted. Because purchase price is low relative to the cost of fixing a bad one, condition and documentation matter far more than mileage or a rare color. A tidy 80k-mile car with receipts beats a 45k-mile survivor with an unknown belt history every time.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt: the 1.6L (B6ZE) and 1.8L (BP) are interference-risk on the 1.8 and generally considered non-interference on the 1.6, but either way the belt, tensioner, water pump and front seals are a 60k-mile/7-year item. Most NAs on the market are overdue. Expect $600–$1,200 done properly with pump and seals; demand a dated receipt, not 'seller says it was done.' 2) Crank nose / crank keyway failure — the 'crank wobble' or short-nose crank issue on 1.6L cars (and some early 1.8s) where the pulley bolt loosens, chews the keyway and destroys the crank snout. Symptoms: wandering timing mark, clunk at idle, wobbling pulley. A trashed crank means engine-out, $2,500–$5,000. Ask whether the pulley bolt was re-torqued to spec (roughly 80–100 lb-ft plus) at the last belt job. 3) Rust — rear wheel arches, rocker panels, front frame rails behind the fenders, floor pans, and especially the rear frame rail near the differential mount and the battery tray corner. Northeast/Midwest cars are frequently structurally rotten under fresh paint. A California car should be clean; still check the rockers and the seam under the rear of the doors. 4) Soft top and rain leaks: original vinyl/cloth tops are 25+ years old, plastic rear windows craze and crack, and zippers fail. Patched tears (as in the example listing) mean a top is due: $400–$900 for a quality cloth top with glass window installed. Leaks track to clogged drain tubes behind the seats — water pools in the floor pans and rots them and the ECU area. 5) Cooling system: 30-year-old radiators (plastic end tanks), brittle hoses, failing thermostats and radiator caps. Overheating on a hot day is common and these engines are tolerant but not immortal. Budget $300–$600 for radiator, hoses, cap, thermostat. 6) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, front crank seal, cam seals, and rear main. The 'oil leak noted' in this listing is typical — valve cover $150, front seals with the timing belt job, rear main $600–$900 with trans out. 7) Suspension bushings and shocks: original bushings are shot at this age; sloppy rear subframe, worn ball joints, torn CV/axle boots, and dead OEM dampers. A full refresh with decent dampers and bushings runs $900–$2,000. 8) Differential and drivetrain: PPF bushings, worn differential mount, leaking diff and transmission seals, and the notorious 5th-gear/2nd-gear synchro wear on high-mile boxes. A crunchy 2nd gear cold is a warning; a rebuilt or used trans is $800–$1,800 installed. Also check the clutch slave cylinder (very common leak, $80 part) and master. 9) Electrics: pop-up headlight motors and linkage (slow or one-eye-up), failing window regulators/motors, worn ignition switch, aged main relay, cracked crank angle sensor O-ring leaking oil, and corroded grounds. Individually cheap, collectively annoying. 10) Interior degradation: sun-baked dashboards crack at the defroster vents, seat bolsters split (especially tan leather on Special Edition/M Edition cars), door card vinyl delaminates, and the plastic rear window scuffs. Dash cap or replacement $200–$600. 11) Brakes and fuel system: seized rear caliper slide pins and parking brake mechanisms, rusty hard lines on non-West-Coast cars, and original fuel pumps/filters that are well past service. 12) Modifications: many NAs have been autocrossed, lowered on cheap coilovers, or fitted with turbo kits. Aftermarket exhaust (as here) may not be CARB-legal for California registration; sway bars and roll bars are benign but raise the question of track use. Look for evidence of an untracked life. 13) Airbag/SRS and the 1990–93 short-nose crank plus 1.6L's smaller brakes are worth noting; 1994+ 1.8L cars gained more power, larger brakes and a stiffer chassis, but also the 1994–95 OBD-I/1996+ OBD-II split which affects California smog testing ease.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt/water pump/tensioner and front seals with a properly torqued crank pulley bolt if no dated receipt exists ($700–$1,200); full fluid service (engine oil, coolant flush, brake fluid, gear oil, diff oil, $300–$500); clutch slave cylinder and a look at the master ($150–$300); clean the soft-top drain tubes and reseal/replace the top if patched ($400–$900); radiator cap, thermostat and hoses if age-unknown ($200–$400); four fresh tires if the current set is over six years old regardless of tread ($500–$800); alignment after any suspension work ($120); fix the noted oil leak, usually valve cover gasket and front seals ($150–$400); new battery and a check of all grounds.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Shock/strut and bushing refresh including rear subframe, control arm and PPF bushings ($900–$2,000); rear main or transmission seal if a leak develops ($600–$900); clutch if it's original and slipping ($800–$1,200 with rear main done at the same time); pop-up headlight motor or linkage repair ($150–$400); window regulator/motor ($150–$300 per side); dash cap or dash replacement if cracked ($200–$600); seat re-bolstering or covers on leather cars ($400–$1,200); brake caliper rebuild/slide pin service and rotors/pads ($400–$700); possible fuel pump, CAS O-ring and ignition refresh (cap, rotor, wires, plugs, $200–$400); catalyst/exhaust restoration to CARB-legal configuration if California smog is a concern ($400–$1,200).
profiles.market_notes: NA prices are driven by rust-free bodies, dated timing belt receipts, originality, and color/trim rarity far more than mileage — clean drivers sit in the $8k–$15k band, sorted 1.8L R-package or low-mile survivors reach $18k–$30k+, and museum-grade 1990 launch cars or pristine BRG Special Editions can exceed that. The 1991 British Racing Green Special Edition (tan leather, Nardi wood, LSD, ~4,000 built) carries a modest premium over a base 1.6, but modifications, a patched top, a noted oil leak and only partial records pull it back toward driver money — which is exactly why the example car landed near $11k. Automatics, non-LSD cars, aftermarket body kits, turbo builds and anything with rocker/rail rust trade at a steep discount. In coastal California, smog-legality of the exhaust and a clean CA title in the seller's name are real value items.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-plus-year-old car needs a deferred-maintenance sweep regardless of mileage: all rubber (belts, hoses, bushings, seals), all fluids, tires by date code, the soft top and its drains, and the cooling system. Budget $2,000–$3,500 in the first year on a clean California example just to bring the consumables current, plus a contingency for a crank/timing surprise on a car with no belt receipt.

profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (NB, 1999-2005, incl. NB1/NB2 and Mazdaspeed)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the NB is a lightweight, analog, top-down driver for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the Laguna Seca area. It is cheap to run when sorted. Condition and history matter far more than badges. The main risk is structural rust, especially on cars from the salt belt or the East Coast, followed by deferred rubber, cooling and timing-belt maintenance on 20-25 year old cars. Favor a documented, unmodified manual car with rust-free rails and a known timing-belt date over low miles alone. Coastal fog makes a good top, working drains and ideally a hardtop worth paying for.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural rust is the number-one NB killer. Look first at the front frame rails where they meet the rocker just behind the front wheels, then the rockers and sills ahead of the rear wheels, the rear wheel-arch lips and the rear subframe mounts. Salt-state cars (this example is from PA) can look fine on top and be rotten underneath. Rail repair runs $1,500-4,000+ and can total the car. Require lift photos of both rails and sills; fresh undercoating or rocker covers over the rails is a red flag.', 'Soft-top drain holes behind the seats clog with debris. Water then backs into the rocker cavities and footwells, causing rust from the inside and damp, mildewed carpet. Check that both drains are clear, carpets and pads are dry, and the cabin has no musty smell. Clearing the drains is free; rust repair from neglected drains is not.', 'The timing belt is due every 60k miles or about 5-7 years, regardless of mileage on a low-use car. The BP 1.8 is generally treated as non-interference in stock form, but a failed belt still strands you. Do the water pump, thermostat, cam and crank seals, and tensioner/idler at the same time. Expect $700-1,200 at an independent shop. Ask for a dated receipt with mileage; without one, budget it immediately.', 'Cooling-system aging is common. The OEM plastic-tank radiator cracks at the seams, the coolant expansion tank yellows and cracks, and hoses and heater hoses go soft. A radiator plus hoses runs $350-800. Look for crusty coolant at the tank seams, low or brown coolant, and temperature creep in traffic.', 'Oil leaks are routine. Expect seepage from the valve cover gasket (including the spark-plug-well seals), the dipstick tube O-ring, and the cam angle sensor (CAS) O-ring at the back of the head. The CAS leak can foul the sensor and cause misfires. Each fix is roughly $100-350. A rear main seal leak shows at the bellhousing drip point and costs $700-1,200 if done with a clutch. Oil in the plug wells points to the valve cover seals.', 'Ignition parts wear out. The coil packs (wasted-spark) crack and cause misfires, especially when hot or damp. Old plug wires leak spark in coastal fog. Coils plus wires and plugs run $200-500.', 'Idle problems are common. A dirty or failing idle air control valve, vacuum leaks from brittle intake hoses, or a sticky throttle body can cause high or hunting idle or stalling. On 2001+ NB2 VVT cars, the oil control valve and VVT system dislike neglected oil changes. Usually $100-400 to sort.', 'Clutch hydraulics and clutch wear: the slave and master cylinders weep or fail, and the clutch can slip at high mileage. Check the throwout bearing for noise and the pivot for wear. A clutch job with seals runs $900-1,600. Check for a soft or high engagement point and for slip in 4th/5th under load.', 'Transmission and driveline: on 5-speeds, look for 2nd/3rd synchro grind (worse when cold) and old gear oil. The 2001+ 6-speed can be notchy and is costlier to rebuild ($2,000-3,500). Bolts and bushings on the PPF (power plant frame) loosen and cause clunks. Differentials leak at the pinion and side seals. Torsen LSD cars carry a premium.', 'Suspension and bushing aging: control-arm bushings crack, shocks are tired (including Bilsteins on Sport/SE cars), and end links and ball joints wear. Symptoms are clunks, vague turn-in and uneven tire wear. A full bushing and shock refresh runs $1,200-2,500; individual items are a few hundred.', 'Soft top aging: the fabric splits at the fold lines and the glass rear window separates from the fabric. The rear defroster grid may fail. Leaks at the header, latches or window seals are common. A quality top installed runs $900-1,800. Coastal fog makes a sound top and the hardtop seals important.', 'Cable-type power window regulators fail and the window motors slow down, at roughly $150-400 per side. The battery is trunk-mounted and must be the vented type with its vent tube connected; a wrong or unvented battery can corrode the trunk floor. Check the tru
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter, coolant (Mazda FL22-type or equivalent), brake/clutch hydraulic flush, transmission GL-4 gear oil, differential gear oil (Torsen-friendly if equipped)', 'Timing belt, water pump, thermostat, seals and tensioner if there is no dated receipt within 60k miles or about 6 years', 'Tires if date codes are over 6 years old, plus a four-wheel alignment', 'Clear the soft-top drains and dry or treat any damp carpet', 'Reseal the valve cover gasket, dipstick tube O-ring and CAS O-ring if seeping', 'Coolant expansion tank and any soft or cracked hoses; pressure-test the radiator', 'Spark plugs, coil inspection and plug wires if old or original', 'Correct vented trunk battery with vent tube attached, plus terminal cleanup']
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Radiator replacement if the OEM plastic tanks are original and stained', 'Clutch hydraulics (slave cylinder, possibly master cylinder) if weeping or spongy', 'Suspension refresh: end links, control-arm bushings, shocks as needed', 'Window regulator on the remaining original side', 'Soft top replacement or reseal and seal kit if the fabric is worn at the folds', 'Idle air control valve cleaning or replacement and vacuum hose refresh', 'Rear main seal or clutch if a bellhousing leak or slip appears', 'Brake pads/rotors and rubber brake hoses on original-hose cars', 'Rust prevention: clean and wax rocker cavities, inspect and treat the frame rails']
profiles.market_notes: Clean, rust-free, unmodified manual cars with records command a premium. Sub-60k-mile examples like the $15,800 example sale show the market rising for top-condition cars, while tired, modified or rusty cars still trade in the $4,000-8,000 range. Prices move most with structural condition and documentation (timing belt and recent service), manual vs. automatic (automatics are heavily discounted), and an included factory hardtop (roughly $1,000-2,000). Special editions (1999 10th Anniversary, SE, Shinsen, Club Spec) and the 2004-2005 Mazdaspeed carry extra value when stock. Desirable colors such as Emerald Mica, Evolution Orange, Crystal Blue and Titanium Gray help. NB2 (2001+) cars bring a little more for VVT and the refreshed interior, but NB1 (1999-2000) is not a meaningful penalty for a driver.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most NBs are now 20-26 years old, so even low-mileage cars usually need a rubber and fluid catch-up: timing belt by age, coolant hoses, expansion tank, radiator, valve cover/CAS seals, clutch hydraulics, tires and bushings. Plan $1,500-3,500 to bring a typical unsorted example to dependable driver status. Structural rust is the one problem that money may not sensibly fix.

profiles.label: Mazda Rotary Pickup (REPU, 1974-1977)
profiles.framing: The REPU is the only rotary-powered pickup ever series-produced, sold only in North America, and roughly 15,000 were built with very few survivors that are not rusty, swapped, or both. For this buyer it is a weekend-and-errands novelty truck with real collector standing, not a load hauler: the 13B makes its case with a 7,000-rpm tach and a howl no small truck has any business making. What matters is a healthy (or honestly documented) rotary, a solid cab/bed/frame, and the survival of the REPU-only sheetmetal and trim that cannot be bought at any price. Engine swaps (13B-REW, 20B, LS) are common and can be well executed, but they change the car from 'documented original' to 'someone's build' and, in California, create a real registration problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Apex seals and rotor housing wear are the defining risk. A tired 13B shows hard hot restarts, blue smoke on startup, low and uneven cranking compression, and a rough idle that smooths above 3,000 rpm. Insist on a rotary-specific compression test (Mazda-style tester reading all three faces per rotor at cranking speed, ideally at operating temperature): each face should be roughly 85-100 psi corrected with no more than about 10-15 psi spread between faces on the same rotor. A proper period 13B rebuild with new seals, re-nitrided or replacement housings, bearings and a rebuilt carb runs $6,000-10,000 today; a 20B or 13B-REW rebuild is $15,000-25,000 with parts that come from wrecked JDM cars.', 'Coolant seals and O-rings between the housings fail with any overheating event. Symptoms are unexplained coolant loss with no external leak, steam or sweet smell at the tailpipe, bubbles/pressure in the overflow, and a hot-start no-start. There is no head-gasket shortcut: it is a full teardown, so this failure is effectively the same cost as a rebuild. Ask for a cooling-system pressure test and a chemical block test for combustion gases in the coolant.', 'Cooling capacity was marginal when new and worse at 50 years old. Original copper/brass radiators are silted, the fan clutch is usually dead, and the thermostat and water pump housing are commonly corroded or cracked. Most healthy survivors have an aluminum radiator and electric fan; a stock-appearing truck with an unrecorded radiator history should be assumed to need a recore ($400-800) or aluminum replacement plus hoses and thermostat ($600-1,200 installed).', 'The thermal reactor exhaust system (a heat-shielded manifold that burned unburnt fuel to meet 1970s emissions) is a known fire and heat-soak hazard. Originals crack, glow red, cook the wiring and firewall insulation, and are effectively unobtainable ($2,000-4,000 if one surfaces). Most trucks have a header and a straight exhaust; that is a functional improvement but an originality loss, and any reactor-delete should be checked for heat shielding, brake line routing, and fuel line proximity.', "The Nikki four-barrel carburetor is the REPU-specific fuel-system weak point: dried accelerator pumps, worn secondary linkage, plugged idle circuits, a seized choke, and a hot-soak percolation problem that mimics flooding. Rebuild kits are scarce ($400-1,200 for a competent rebuild) and many trucks run Holley/Weber or EFI conversions. Ask what carb is fitted and whether idle/part-throttle air-fuel has actually been checked, not just 'it runs'.", "Oil metering pump (OMP) status is the single cheapest question with the biggest consequence. If the OMP has been blocked off or disconnected, the engine MUST be premixed (roughly 2-4 oz of two-stroke or 10W30 per gallon) at every fill, forever. Ask directly for the premix routine and receipts for oil; a blocked OMP plus a seller who says 'you don't need to premix' is an apex-seal timebomb. A functioning OMP should be verified for flow at the injection lines.", 'Rust is the usual reason a REPU is not worth saving. Check cab corners, the lower rear cab panel and rear window channel (the 1977 bumped-out window in particular traps water), floor pans under the rubber/carpet, the seat riser and cab mounts, the inner and outer bedsides behind the REPU-only flares, the front fender bottoms, the battery box on the right bedside (acid rot), and the frame rails at the rear spring hangers and above the axle. Cab corner and floor repair with correct fabrication is $3,000-8,000 in bodywork, and there are no reproduction REPU panels.', "REPU-only trim is unobtainium: the eggcrate grille, fender flares, round taillights, 'Rotary Pickup/Rotary Engine' badging and tailgate lettering, the rotary-specific instrument cluster with 7,000-rpm tach, the bumpers, and the 1977 rear-window glass. Missing or damaged pieces can cost thousands on the collector market or stall a project indefinitely. Photograph and inventory e
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including a coolant flush with correct rotary-safe coolant; new thermostat, hoses, and cap; complete brake hydraulic refresh (flex lines, wheel cylinders or caliper seals, master, fluid); replace all rubber fuel line with SAE 30R9 and check the tank and sender; tires almost always need replacing on date code alone even with good tread; ignition tune (plugs, wires, points/condenser or coil check, timing set with a light on both leading and trailing); establish and document a premix routine if the OMP is blocked; belts, battery, and a full lighting/grounds sweep; leak-check the radiator and lower housing and plan an aluminum radiator/electric fan if the truck runs hot in traffic; seat belts and steering-play assessment before it is driven on Highway 1. Budget $3,000-6,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main/front cover seals if the engine is out for anything; four-speed second-gear synchro or a documented five-speed conversion; leaf springs, shackle bushings, shocks, and U-joints; steering box and drag-link refresh; exhaust fabrication or heat shielding done properly; carburetor rebuild or a documented tune of whatever induction is fitted; localized rust repair at cab corners, bedsides, and battery box before it spreads; radiator recore; wiring harness repairs where heat has cooked the insulation; and a compression retest at the 12-month mark to trend seal health. Budget $4,000-9,000 on a good truck, far more if the engine has to come out.
profiles.market_notes: Condition and originality drive REPU money far more than mileage, which is unverifiable on a five-digit odometer and largely irrelevant on a rebuilt rotary. Rust-free Southwest/California survivors with complete REPU-only trim, original 13B, correct gauges, and a documented history are the top of the market; well-executed 20B/13B-REW builds with named builders and standalone tunes can match or exceed that number with a narrower buyer pool and no smog path in CA. Long-bed 1977 cars with the bumped-out rear window have their own following as the final-year variant. Discounts come fast for rust, missing grille/flares/taillights/badges, non-rotary swaps (LS), automatic conversions, and 'ran when parked' engines; expect roughly $20,000-30,000 for a driver, $35,000-55,000 for an excellent original or a strong documented build, and $60,000+ only for concours-grade originals.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume everything rubber and every fluid is due regardless of what the seller says: fuel hose, brake hydraulics, coolant, radiator, hoses, bushings, and tires on date code alone. A 50-year-old low-production Japanese truck also needs a wiring and grounds sweep and a fuel-tank inspection before it is trusted on a mountain road, and any rotary with unknown seal history should be priced with a rebuild reserve set aside from day one.

profiles.label: Mercedes-Benz SL-Class R107 (350SL/450SL/380SL/560SL, 1971-1989)
profiles.framing: The R107 is a heavy, overbuilt two-seat convertible for top-down cruising on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not a sports car. It is simple enough for an independent shop to keep on the road. The price is set almost entirely by structural rust, the health of the timing chain and fuel injection, and whether the car passes California smog. US cars were automatic-only, so an automatic is normal here and not a compromise. A 1979 450SL at the bottom of the market is only a bargain if the floors, sills and chain guides check out, because body rot and a jumped chain can each cost more than the car.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural rust is the number-one killer. Inspect the rocker panels, the four jacking points, the front and rear floor pans (especially under the carpets behind the seats), the rear wheel-arch lips, and the trunk floor and spare-tire well. Also check the lower windshield frame and A-pillar bases, where the cowl and windshield seal leak. Bubbles under the chrome trim and around the headlight buckets usually mean far worse underneath. Proper metal repair on sills and floors runs $3,000-10,000+. Look for underbody photos from a lift and ask whether the carpets have ever been pulled.', 'Clogged soft-top well and cowl drains send water into the cabin and trunk. Wet or musty carpets, rusty seat-rail bolts and a water line in the spare-tire well are warning signs of hidden floor rot.', 'Timing chain guide rails (M117 V8) become brittle with age and break regardless of mileage. Pieces can drop into the oil pan, and the chain can jump and bend valves. Guides, tensioner and chain cost roughly $1,200-3,000; valve damage pushes a repair to $4,000-7,000. Ask for dated receipts for guides and chain, ideally within the last 60k miles or 15 years. If there are none, budget for the job immediately. On 1981-83 380SLs, also confirm the original single-row chain was converted to double-row.', 'Camshaft lobe and rocker-arm wear is common on 4.5 and 3.8 V8s, often from oil spray-bar problems or long oil-change intervals. Symptoms are ticking at idle and lost power. Cams and rockers run about $2,000-4,000. Look for oil-change records and ask whether anyone has inspected the cams with the valve covers off.', 'Valve stem seals harden with age and cause a puff of blue smoke on a cold start or after idling. Replacing them with the heads on the engine costs about $900-1,800. Watch the cold start in person or on video.', 'The Bosch K-Jetronic (CIS) mechanical fuel injection (1976-on US cars; 1972-75 used D-Jetronic) causes hard hot starts, cold-start stumble and poor idle. The usual culprits are the warm-up regulator, cold-start valve, fuel accumulator, fuel pump, fuel distributor, injector seals and vacuum leaks. Rust from a tank that sat unused contaminates the whole system. Baseline tuning costs $300-800; a distributor, regulator or accumulator can reach $1,500-3,000. Look for fuel-system receipts and a smog printout showing emissions numbers.', 'California smog applies. Model-year 1976 and newer cars are not exempt, and the seller must supply a smog certificate that is less than 90 days old. Missing or rusted catalytic converters, air-injection pumps and vacuum-controlled emissions parts, plus a rich-running CIS, cause failures. Emissions repairs typically run $500-2,500 and can be more if a CARB-legal catalytic converter is needed.', 'The three-speed automatic has several known faults. A leaking vacuum modulator pulls transmission fluid into the intake, causing smoke and low fluid. Other symptoms of wear are harsh or late shifts, slipping, and delayed engagement. A rebuild costs $2,500-4,500. Check that the fluid is red and not burnt, and look for any service history.', 'Driveline rubber ages out. The driveshaft flex discs, center support bearing, and engine and transmission mounts deteriorate, causing clunks when shifting into gear and vibration at speed. Expect $400-1,200.', 'Front-end wear shows up as wander and a loose steering feel. The usual causes are front lower ball joints, upper and lower control-arm bushings, the idler-arm bushing, tie rods, the steering damper, play in the steering box, and rear subframe and trailing-arm bushings. Suspension refreshes run $800-3,000.', 'Cooling-system age can overheat these heavy V8s in inland heat. Weak points are the original radiator (plastic tanks on later cars), water pump, viscous fan clutch and hoses. Expect $500-1,500. Look for a steady temperature gauge and a history of coolant service.', 'Electrical and instrument faults are common. The ceramic fuse box corrodes, and window motors and regulato
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid service: engine oil and filter, transmission fluid and filter, differential oil, power-steering fluid, coolant flush, and brake fluid flush', 'Fuel filter replacement plus a CIS baseline: fuel pressure test, warm-up regulator and cold-start valve check, vacuum-leak smoke test, and idle/mixture set', 'Timing chain, guide and tensioner inspection with the valve covers off (and replacement if there are no receipts)', 'Belts, radiator and heater hoses, and vacuum lines', 'Tires by date code (anything over 6-7 years old gets replaced regardless of tread)', 'Brake inspection: caliper function, rubber hoses, and pad and rotor condition', 'Clearing the soft-top well and cowl drains, and checking the trunk and floors for standing water', 'Inspection of the driveshaft flex discs, center
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Front-end refresh: ball joints, control-arm bushings, idler arm, tie rods and steering damper', 'Valve stem seals if the car smokes on startup', 'Engine and transmission mounts plus the driveshaft flex discs', 'Cooling-system refresh: radiator, water pump and fan clutch as needed', 'Soft-top replacement or pad and weatherstrip renewal', 'CIS parts as needed: accumulator, fuel pump, injector seals and warm-up regulator', 'A/C repair or R134a conversion, plus vacuum-actuator repair for climate and central locking', 'Speedometer and odometer gear repair', 'Door, window and hardtop weatherseals']
profiles.market_notes: The 560SL (1986-89) commands the highest prices, especially with low miles, followed by the 380SL. The US 450SL, especially 1976-80 CIS cars with smaller bumpers, is the cheapest entry point. Rough examples trade at $6,000-10,000, good drivers at $12,000-20,000, and exceptional documented cars well above that. A rust-free California history, the factory hardtop, a good soft top, working A/C and a thick folder of records move price the most. Silver, red, black and white with black or tan interiors sell better than 1970s greens and browns. Mileage matters less than documentation because odometers often fail. Aftermarket wheels, European-style bumper conversions or removed emissions equipment reduce value and can make smog compliance impossible.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most R107s have spent decades with sporadic use, so expect to renew essentially all rubber: hoses, mounts, bushings, flex discs, seals and tires. Also expect to baseline the CIS system and address timing chain guides that are brittle with age even at modest miles. Budget $3,000-6,000 of catch-up on a typical driver-grade car before counting any rust, top or transmission work.
