profiles.label: Mercury Capri / Capri XR2 (Australian-built SA30, 1991-1994)
profiles.framing: The 1991-94 Capri was built by Ford Australia on Mazda 323 (BF-era) mechanicals. The XR2 adds the 132-hp turbocharged, intercooled Mazda B6T 1.6 DOHC, almost always with a 5-speed. For this buyer it is a cheap, light, fun top-down runabout for coastal roads, not an investment. What matters is a dry, rust-free tub, a healthy turbo engine with a known timing-belt history, a sound top, and good original suspension and trim. Capri-specific body, trim and suspension parts are scarce or unobtainable, so a complete, unmolested car is worth far more than a cheap project.
profiles.weak_points: ["Water intrusion and floor rust: leaking soft-top seals, windshield-header and door-glass seals, and clogged body drains let water into the footwells. That soaks the carpet and padding, then rusts the floor pans, seat-mount areas and the lower A-pillar and sill junction. Fogged gauges, mildew smell or rusty seat bolts are red flags. Floor-pan and sill repair runs $1,500-4,000+ and can exceed the car's value. Ask for photos of the underside, the footwells with carpet lifted, and the spare-tire well.", 'Convertible top and hardtop: the top fabric, rear window and frame pivots wear, and latches and weatherstrips shrink. Hardtops fade and their seals and mounting hardware go missing. An aftermarket top is roughly $400-800 for the part plus $400-800 to install. Capri-specific weatherstrip is hard to source, and a good used hardtop is scarce.', 'Timing belt and water pump on the B6T: the interval is 60k miles or about 7 years, and most cars are overdue by age even at low miles. Treat the belt as unknown without a dated receipt. Budget $500-900 for belt, tensioner, water pump, cam and crank seals, and the CAS O-ring.', "Crank pulley and keyway wear: B6-family engines of this era (compare the early 1.6 Miata 'short-nose' crank) can develop crank-pulley wobble from keyway wear. That shows up as a wobbling pulley, timing scatter or belt walk. Caught early it means pulley bolt and keyway service at $200-500. If neglected, it can mean a crankshaft or engine at $1,500-3,500.", 'Turbocharger and boost plumbing: the original turbo can suffer worn shaft seals (blue smoke on startup or decel, oily intercooler piping), shaft play, coked oil feed and return lines, and cracked boost or vacuum hoses that cause low or erratic boost. A rebuild or replacement runs $800-1,800. Hose refresh is $150-400. Look for any service records and an unmodified boost-control setup.', 'Oil leaks and cooling system: valve-cover gasket, cam seals, CAS O-ring and oil-pan leaks are common. The original radiator with plastic tanks, the heater hoses and the thermostat are age-expired, and overheating risks a head gasket ($1,200-2,000). A cooling refresh is $400-800.', 'Clutch hydraulics and clutch: master and slave cylinders weep with age, and the turbo torque wears clutches, especially if previous owners abused it. A clutch job runs $800-1,300 and hydraulics $250-500. Watch for slipping in 3rd and 4th under boost, or a high, soft or sinking pedal.', 'Transaxle and driveline: worn 2nd and 3rd synchros (grinding on fast shifts) and sloppy shift-linkage bushings are common. Torn CV boots lead to clicking outer CV joints. Bushings and CV axles run $200-700. A used transaxle runs $800-1,500 installed.', 'Suspension parts scarcity: Capri-specific struts, strut mounts, springs and rear suspension bushings are hard or impossible to find new, and some cars have mismatched Mazda 323 or Festiva substitutes. Worn struts mean floaty, bouncy behavior or clunks. Good original suspension is a real plus, and sorting a tired setup can cost $600-1,500 plus parts hunting.', 'Electrical aging: pop-up headlight motors and linkages, slow power windows and tired regulators, and door-lock actuators all fail. Corroded grounds affect gauges and fuel-injection behavior. Original-style ECUs of this era can suffer leaking capacitors. Individual fixes run $100-500 each. A sorted car is worth a premium.', 'Air conditioning: the original R-12 system is likely leaking or empty. Recharging or converting to R-134a with a compressor, drier and seals runs $800-1,500, so many owners skip it.', 'Airbag and SRS (driver airbag wheel): a 30+-year-old airbag module, clockspring and crash sensors may set an SRS light. Parts are scarce, so note the warning-lamp status. Diagnosis and repair can cost $300-1,000 if parts are even available.', "Interior and trim plastics: brittle door handles, console and dash plastics crack and break. Seat fabric and bolsters wear, and Capri-unique badges, spoilers, lenses and side m
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Timing belt, tensioner, water pump, cam and crank seals, and CAS O-ring unless there is a dated receipt within about 5 years ($500-900)', 'Engine oil and filter, coolant flush, brake fluid flush, clutch fluid flush, and transaxle fluid change ($250-450)', 'All rubber boost, vacuum, coolant and heater hoses, inspected and likely replaced ($200-500)', 'Tires replaced if older than about 6 years, regardless of tread ($400-600)', 'Top and door seals cleaned and treated, body drains cleared, and leaks water-tested ($100-300 DIY, more if seals are needed)', 'Brake service: pads, rotors as needed, hoses if cracked, and caliper slide service ($300-700)', 'California smog check, registration and VIN verification, plus any emissions fixes needed to pass ($100-600)', 'Battery, ground straps and pop
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch master and slave cylinders, and the clutch itself if slipping or high-engagement ($250-1,300)', 'Radiator, thermostat and cooling refresh ($400-800)', 'Valve-cover and oil-pan gasket reseal ($200-500)', 'CV axles or boots and shift-linkage bushings ($200-700)', 'Struts, mounts and bushings if available ($600-1,500)', 'Convertible top or rear window replacement if shrunk or leaking ($800-1,600 installed)', 'AC conversion or recharge if desired ($800-1,500)', 'Power window regulator and motor, plus pop-up headlight motor repairs ($150-600)', 'Turbo oil feed and return lines and boost-control check, or a turbo rebuild if smoking ($150-1,800)']
profiles.market_notes: These are inexpensive cars: driver XR2s commonly trade in the low-to-mid four figures, and only exceptionally clean, low-mile, documented examples push higher. The XR2 turbo with a 5-speed carries a clear premium over the base non-turbo or automatic Capri. A rust-free floor, an intact top, the original removable hardtop, and complete, uncracked Capri-specific trim and spoilers move price more than color does. Low documented mileage, timing-belt receipts and an unmodified engine add value, while rust, a missing hardtop, aftermarket modifications or missing trim cut it sharply because parts are so scarce.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even low-mile examples are 30+ years old, so assume all rubber is expired unless receipts prove otherwise: timing belt, hoses, seals, top weatherstrip, bushings and tires. Plan roughly $1,500-3,000 of catch-up work in the first year. Rust or a water-damaged interior can quickly push repair costs past the car's market value.

profiles.label: Porsche 911 (964) Carrera 2 / Carrera 4
profiles.framing: The 964 is the last usable-everyday air-cooled 911 with modern comforts (power steering, ABS, coil springs, real HVAC) and the raw M64 3.6 character that later cars smooth out. For a Carmel-based driver, this is a weekend Highway 1 and Laureles Grade car that can be driven hard without the anxiety of a six-figure 993 Turbo or a museum-grade 2.7 RS — but only if the engine's known sealing and top-end issues are documented as already addressed. The Carrera 4's extra driveline (front diff, transfer shaft, ABD/ABS hydraulics) adds capability and complexity; a well-sorted C4 is a superb all-weather coastal car, a neglected one is a money pit. Documented, unmodified, with a legible chain of invoices matters far more here than mileage or cosmetics.
profiles.weak_points: Engine case/cylinder oil leaks: the M64's biggest single issue is leaking head studs and, more famously, the dual-row-to-single-row era case and the notorious oil return tube and cylinder-to-case seepage. Most honest 964s weep from the through-bolt/head-stud area and the chain housing gaskets; a proper fix is engine-out, roughly $12,000–$25,000+ depending on whether cylinders/pistons and heads are touched. Look for an engine-out invoice naming head studs (ARP or Raceware), Carrillo/ARP rod bolts, and resealing of the chain housings and cam towers. Dual-mass flywheel: early cars (1989–1991) used a Freudenberg DMF that fails and clatters at idle; later LuK units are better. Failure symptoms are rattle at idle that disappears on clutch engagement; replacement is a transmission-out job, $2,500–$4,500 with clutch. Distributor vent belt (the internal belt linking the twin distributor rotors): if it snaps, the secondary rotor runs unsynchronized, torching the cap and potentially the engine. Later factory vented caps mitigate; there must be a receipt in the last 4–6 years / 30–40k miles or plan $600–$1,200 to inspect and renew. Valve guides and top-end wear: high-mileage M64s (over 100k) smoke on startup and burn oil; a leakdown/compression test is not optional. Head gaskets and studs pulling on high-heat, hard-driven cars are a five-figure repair. Oil cooler and lines: the front-fender-mounted oil cooler and long steel/rubber oil lines corrode and weep; a leaking cooler dumps oil quickly and costs $700–$1,800 plus lines. Air conditioning: original R12 systems converted poorly to R134a are the norm; condensers, evaporator, and hoses all age out and full restoration with a modern condenser/parallel-flow setup runs $2,000–$4,000. Carrera 4 specific: the front differential and transfer/center driveshaft leak and the ABD/PDAS hydraulic unit and its accumulator fail — a failed C4 hydraulic pump or pressure accumulator triggers ABS/brake warning lights and parts are scarce and expensive ($1,500–$4,000). C4 front CV/axle boots and the front driveshaft support are common leak points. Motor/transmission mounts sag (many owners fit 993-spec mounts, as this car has), causing shifter vibration. Suspension bushings, control-arm ball joints, and rear spring plate bushings are all 30 years old on original cars; a full refresh with Bilsteins runs $3,000–$6,000. Airbag/pedal box: the 964 pedal cluster bushings wear and the clutch pedal bracket cracks — a known and cheap-to-fix but commonly ignored item. Electrics: the alarm/central locking control unit, power window regulators, HVAC control head (blend flap servos and the vacuum-operated system) and instrument cluster board solder joints all fail; the odometer gears crack and the speedo needs a rebuild ($400–$800). Rust: 964s are galvanized and generally sound, but check the front trunk floor/battery tray, the sunroof drains and the A-pillar corners, the base of the windshield (leaks from resealed or replaced windshields cause rot under the dash), and the rear torsion tube area. Fuel system: rubber fuel hoses and the fuel-line rail under the tank harden; fire risk on cars without replacement records. Finally, at 150k+ miles the five-speed G64 transaxle's second-gear synchro wears — notchy 2nd on a cold car is normal, a crunch under load is not; a rebuild is $5,000–$8,000.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (Mobil 1 15W-50 or equivalent, ~11 quarts, filter, drain plug seals), valve adjustment if not documented within 15k miles, new fuel filter, inspect and likely replace the distributor vent belt and both caps/rotors if the receipt is older than five years, replace hardened fuel and vacuum hoses, four-wheel alignment after any suspension work, check and correct tire age (anything over six years replaced regardless of tread), A/C evacuate/recharge and leak test, and a full diagnostic scan of the DME and — on a C4 — the ABS/ABD hydraulic system. Expect to chase at least one small oil leak (chain housing, oil return tubes, or a cooler line) and to service or rebuild the pedal box bushings.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and dual-mass flywheel if not recently replaced, motor and transmission mounts if still original, front and rear shock/strut refresh and rubber bushings if undocumented, oil cooler and hard lines if any seepage, A/C condenser and hoses for reliable coastal-summer function, power window regulators and central locking control unit, HVAC blend/flap servos, brake flex lines and full fluid flush (and ABS accumulator on the C4 if pressure warning appears), and on higher-mileage cars a transaxle reseal and possible 2nd-gear synchro attention. Budget for a set of correct-size Michelin or Pirelli N-rated tires and a proper corner-balance/alignment.
profiles.market_notes: Coupes with a manual outsell Tiptronics by a wide margin and Tiptronic C2s trade at a steep discount; Carrera 4 coupes historically sat below C2s but factory widebody (Turbo-look, option M491) cars are genuinely rare and command a large premium, as do RS Americas, Turbos, and Speedsters. Documented engine-out top-end work with head studs is worth real money and its absence should be priced in at $15,000–$25,000 regardless of how the car presents. Original paint and matching numbers matter, but a well-executed, fully invoiced refurbishment with photos from a known shop is acceptable to a driver-buyer; unverifiable 'restored' claims, respray over filler, and mileage discrepancies (or a Carfax that misidentifies the model, as in the example listing) are where money is lost. High-mileage cars are acceptable at the right price if the service chain is continuous; six-figure asks on a 170k-mile C4 rest entirely on the quality and verifiability of the rebuild paperwork.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 30-plus-year-old 964 needs everything rubber renewed: fuel and vacuum hoses, brake flex lines, engine and transmission mounts, suspension bushings, window and door seals, and the A/C system. Even a freshly refurbished example will need a shakedown cycle of fluid services, a valve adjustment, alignment, and chasing small leaks over the first few thousand miles, plus tires if the date codes are past six years.

profiles.label: Porsche 911 Carrera (993, naturally aspirated)
profiles.framing: The 993 is the last air-cooled 911. For this buyer it is a usable, analog weekend and canyon car on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not a garage queen. The most important questions are the health of the cylinder heads and valve guides, and whether the car will pass a California smog check and register cleanly. That matters for any out-of-state car, and especially for 1996-98 OBD-II cars with the secondary air injection (SAI) problem. Documented, unmodified, rust-free examples with a clear oil-consumption and leakdown story are worth a real premium over cheaper cars with unknown top ends.
profiles.weak_points: ["Valve guide wear is the big-ticket 993 failure. It typically shows at 70k-130k miles, earlier on cars that sat or were driven gently. Symptoms are blue smoke on cold start or after idling at lights, oil use worse than about 1 qt per 1,000 miles, and a fouled plug or two. Leakdown can look acceptable while the guides are worn, so a guide 'wiggle' check needs the engine apart. A top-end rebuild (heads, guides, valves, gaskets) runs $12k-$22k at a good independent and much more with machine-shop surprises. Look for receipts naming the specific work: guides, valve job, head gaskets.", 'Secondary air injection (SAI) on 1996-98 OBD-II cars. Carbon clogs the small air passages in the cylinder heads, setting P0410/P0411 and a check-engine light, which fails a California smog check. In-car port cleaning or drilling costs $1,500-$4,000 and does not always last. The permanent fix is heads-off, usually combined with a top-end job. Ask for proof the SAI monitor has been run and passed, not just codes cleared before the sale.', 'Oil leaks are near-universal on age. Common sources are the lower valve cover gaskets, chain housing covers, the oil return tubes between case and heads, the oil pressure sender and switch, the oil cooler seals, and the rear main seal. Leaks on hot exhaust or heat exchangers create smoke and smell. Valve cover reseals cost $800-$2,000. A rear main seal needs the transmission out ($1,500-$2,500, more if a clutch is done at the same time). Look for recent reseal receipts and photos of a dry underside.', 'Front oil cooler, lines, and fan. The right-front fender oil cooler, its long hard lines to the engine, and the thermostatically controlled cooler fan corrode and fail with age. Watch for corroded or weeping line fittings, oil residue in the right-front wheel well, and a fan that never cycles when hot. Lines cost $1,500-$3,000 installed. A cooler or fan costs $400-$1,200.', 'Manual cars: the dual-mass flywheel (DMF) and clutch. DMF wear shows as rattle at idle that stops when the clutch is pressed, plus chatter on take-off. Clutch and DMF together cost about $3,000-$4,500. Also check the shift linkage bushings and the clutch hydraulics. The 6-speed G50/21 gearbox is otherwise robust; check for second- and third-gear synchro crunch on fast shifts.', 'Tiptronic cars: the 4-speed Tiptronic S is generally durable but ages. Watch for harsh or delayed 1-2 and 2-3 shifts, flare on upshift, slipping, delayed engagement into D or R, and electronic faults that disable Tip mode. Much depends on fluid service history. A rebuild or valve-body repair runs $4,000-$8,000. Tiptronic also cuts resale value sharply, which is a cost if the buyer ever sells.', "Rust is limited on this galvanized body, but it does exist. The classic 993 rust is in the windshield and rear window frame corners under the seals. Repair requires glass removal, metal work, and paint ($3,000-$8,000). Also check the front trunk floor, battery box, door bottoms, and the area near the fuel tank. Carmel's salt air makes later bubbling a real concern. Corner rust visible in photos usually means more under the seal.", 'Ignition and DME. The 993 is twin-plug with twin distributors. Distributor cap, rotor, and drive-belt wear, along with moisture buildup, cause misfires; a vent kit and distributor service cost $500-$1,500. Twelve plugs and wires cost $900-$1,600 because of labor. The DME relay is a classic no-start or stalling cause; carry a $50-$100 spare.', '1996+ alarm, immobilizer, and central locking. Remote fob, alarm module, and immobilizer faults cause no-start and intermittent locking problems. Check that all keys and fobs work and that the immobilizer releases reliably. A replacement fob with programming costs $300-$800. Module repair costs $300-$1,000.', 'Climate control. The automatic heater controller fails (the example car just had it replaced). Other failures include the heater flap cables and actuators, heater blower motor ($600-$1,200), and auxiliary f
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['California smog pre-check or OBD-II readiness scan before or immediately after purchase. Resolve any SAI or catalytic converter codes before registration deadlines.', 'Engine oil and filter with the correct air-cooled spec oil; check oil level hot, on level ground, idling.', 'Transmission fluid: gear oil for manuals, or Tiptronic ATF plus final-drive oil, if not documented in the last 2 years.', 'Brake fluid flush and inspection of pads, rotors, and hoses.', 'Fan belt and alternator belt inspection or replacement, plus the AC belt.', 'Spare DME relay. Inspect the distributor cap, rotor, and vent, and the condition of the plugs and wires.', 'Battery and charging-system check; fit a battery maintainer if the car will sit.', 'Tire age check by DOT date; replace if over 6 years, regardless o
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Valve cover gasket, chain cover, and oil return tube reseal if leaking.', 'Spark plugs and plug wires (12) if not documented in the last 30k miles or 5 years.', 'Distributor service and vent kit if not previously done.', 'Front oil cooler line replacement if the fittings are corroded or weeping.', 'Suspension refresh: shocks, front control arm and rear LSA bushings, strut mounts, engine and transmission mounts.', 'AC service, front condenser fan, and possible condenser or evaporator work.', 'Heater blower and heater flap cable or actuator repairs.', 'Window regulators, sunroof cable and drain service, and rear spoiler motor or cable service.', 'Manual cars: plan for a clutch and DMF if rattle or chatter is present.', 'Corrosion treatment of the windshield and rear window corners if early
profiles.market_notes: Transmission is the biggest single value lever. Manual 6-speed Carrera coupes trade at roughly a 35-50% premium over Tiptronic cars, and Tip coupes sit at the bottom of the coupe market. Wide-body Carrera S and Carrera 4S (and the Targa to some collectors) carry big premiums over a base Carrera 2; Cabriolets trade lower. Paint-to-sample and desirable colors such as Speed Yellow, Riviera Blue, Arena Red, and Guards Red outperform silver and black. Mileage bands below 50k and 50-90k move price, but a documented top end (guides and SAI), a dry engine, no rust, and a clean ownership history matter more for a driver. Many owners, repossession or title anomalies, and visible corner rust should pull the price down materially.
profiles.catchup_notes: Most 993s are 27-30 years old, and even well-kept ones need some age-related catch-up: rubber (seals, bushings, mounts, boots), oil leak reseals, ignition service, climate-control repairs, and fluids. A typical example with incomplete records should be budgeted at $5,000-$10,000 of catch-up work in the first year, on top of the risk reserve for a top end or SAI fix. Out-of-state cars also need to clear California smog before registration, so SAI and catalyst health should be confirmed up front.

profiles.label: Porsche 944 Turbo / Turbo S (951, 1986–1991)
profiles.framing: The 951 is the sharpest-driving front-engine Porsche of the era: 2.5L turbo four, rear transaxle, near-50/50 balance, and in Turbo S trim the M030 suspension, 40% limited-slip, and 928 S4 brakes that make it genuinely quick on a real road. For a Carmel-based driver this is a weekend-and-occasional-commute car that rewards mechanical sympathy and punishes deferred maintenance more than almost anything else from the 1980s. What matters is not mileage on the odometer but the last five years of receipts: belts, rollers, water pump, cooling system, torque tube, and a clean compression/leak-down. Coastal humidity and salt-air storage mean the battery box, sunroof drains, and hatch surround deserve as much attention as the engine.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt and balance-shaft belt with their rollers and tensioner: the M44/52 is an interference engine and a snapped or jumped belt bends valves and can crack the head — budget $6,000–12,000 for the repair versus $900–1,800 for the preventive service. Service interval is realistically 30,000 miles or 4 years regardless of miles; demand a dated, mileage-stamped invoice, ideally with a belt-tension-gauge reading noted. Low-mileage cars are the highest risk here because owners defer on miles, not years. 2) Water pump and thermostat housing: pumps seize or leak from the weep hole and take the timing belt with them — always replaced with belts; plastic/alloy housings and the coolant crossover corrode. 3) Cylinder head cracking between the valve seats and head-gasket failure on any car that has been overheated or run lean/overboosted — symptoms are coolant loss with no external leak, pressurized expansion tank, sweet exhaust smell. A used head plus machine work and gasket set runs $3,500–6,000. 4) Oil cooler O-rings/seals at the block leak oil into coolant or coolant into oil — look for mayonnaise on the filler cap and at the cooler seams; a straightforward $400–800 job if caught early. 5) Turbocharger: K26/6 (Turbo) or K26/8 (Turbo S) shaft play, coked oil feed line, and failing oil return gasket cause blue smoke on overrun and boost loss. Rebuilt cartridges/units run $1,500–3,000 installed; the oil feed line should be replaced any time the turbo is. 6) Boost-control system: the wastegate diaphragm, KLR cycling valve, and a web of aging rubber vacuum and boost hoses crack and cause soft boost, overboost cutout, or surge. A full silicone/rubber hose refresh and wastegate rebuild is $400–1,200. 7) Torque tube bearings and center support: a resonant droning/whirring at 2,000–3,500 rpm that changes with clutch engagement; rebuild or replacement is $1,500–3,500 because the transaxle and tube must come out. 8) Clutch: the rubber-centered disc degrades with age and the pressure plate/pilot bearing go with it; do the torque tube, rear main seal, and clutch together — $2,500–4,500 as a package. 9) Front suspension: the one-piece control arms with integral ball joints and the aging bushings produce vague steering and clunks; arms are $300–700 each plus alignment. Turbo S Koni adjustables often seize or leak and are expensive to replace or rebuild ($1,200–2,500 for a set). Rear torsion bar tube bushings and seized torsion adjusters make ride-height correction a job. 10) Brakes: Turbo S (and 1989 Turbo) use 928 S4 four-piston calipers and larger rotors — parts are pricier and some rotors are becoming scarce; seized pistons and crusty ABS lines are common on stored cars. Full four-corner refresh with rotors and rebuilt calipers is $2,000–3,500. The Bosch ABS system's sensors and the hydraulic unit can be costly and hard to source. 11) Electrical gremlins: the DME/fuel pump relay is a classic no-start, ground strap corrosion causes random faults, and the VDO instrument cluster's odometer gears strip — which is exactly why so many 944s carry 'Not Actual Mileage' or mileage-inconsistency entries. A branded NAM title is permanent and materially affects value. 12) Interior consumables: cracked dash pads ($800–2,000 to replace/recover), sagging headliner and sunroof cassette, failing window regulators and motors, disintegrating door-card and rear-hatch trim, and vacuum-operated HVAC controls that stop working when the pod diaphragms fail. 13) Air conditioning: original R12 systems either converted or dead; evaporator replacement means dash-out labor at $1,500–2,500. 14) Rust and water: bodies are galvanized so rot is not endemic, but check the battery box and the floor/frame rail under it (acid), sunroof drain exits, the rear hatch surround and hinge area, the fuel tank/torsion tube area, jack points, and the inner fenders behind the front wheels. Also inspect for aged fuel hoses under the intake and at the fuel rail — 1980s rubber plus turbo h
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service if not documented within 12 months (engine oil, transaxle, brake fluid, coolant); DME and fuel pump relay replacement plus a spare; replacement of any rubber fuel line under the intake and at the rail; rubber/vacuum and boost hose refresh with new clamps; tires if older than 6 years regardless of tread (very common on low-use 951s); battery, ground straps, and a battery-box cleanup; front-end alignment; and if belt documentation is thin or older than 4 years, an immediate timing/balance belt, roller, tensioner, water pump and thermostat service. Expect $2,500–5,000 in the first 30 days on a typical documented car and more if belts are unknown.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch, rear main seal, and torque tube bearings as a combined job if any driveline drone or clutch shudder is present; oil cooler seals and valve-cover/cam-tower gasket leaks; wastegate diaphragm and boost-control refresh; brake caliper rebuild plus rotors and stainless lines; Koni damper rebuild or replacement and rear torsion-bar bushings; motor and transaxle mounts; A/C recharge or evaporator/condenser work; window regulator and sunroof mechanism service; and cosmetic catch-up on dash, seat bolsters, and rear hatch struts. A realistic 12-month figure is $4,000–9,000 depending on what the PPI finds.
profiles.market_notes: The 1988 Turbo S (about 1,000 US cars, including the Silver Rose edition) and the 1989 Turbo that inherited S mechanicals sit well above standard 1986–1988 Turbos, and a Porsche Certificate of Authenticity confirming S equipment is effectively required to claim the premium. Documented belt/water-pump service, original paint, correct 16" Club Sport wheels, a working A/C, and unmolested boost/ECU are the value drivers; chipped/overboosted cars, cut dashes, and aftermarket turbo or intercooler swaps push buyers away. Mileage bands matter but only when the odometer is credible — a 'Not Actual Mileage' or mileage-inconsistency brand should discount a car meaningfully (commonly 15–30%) versus an equivalent clean-title example, because it is permanent and follows the car. Manual-only market; color and interior condition (especially an uncracked dash and unfaded leatherette) swing the last 10%.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-plus-year-old car needs a rubber and fluid reset regardless of mileage: every vacuum, boost, coolant, and fuel hose, belts and pump on age not miles, tires, brake fluid and flexlines, and motor mounts. Low-mileage examples are often worse in this respect than driven ones — seals dry out, fuel systems varnish, and Konis seize from sitting. Budget $3,000–6,000 of age-related catch-up in year one even on a well-presented car.

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster (981, incl. S / GTS / Spyder)
profiles.framing: The 981 is the sweet spot of modern Boxsters: the last naturally aspirated flat-six mid-engine Porsche roadster, with electric steering that is still genuinely good, a stiff aluminum-intensive chassis, and no IMS bearing to worry about. For a Carmel-based driver this is a near-ideal Highway 1 / Laureles Grade weekend car that can also be driven daily in the region's mild climate, with the caveat that it is a two-seat convertible with two small trunks. What matters here is a documented, unmodified-or-reversible example with a full Porsche/independent service file, a healthy convertible top mechanism, and evidence the engine has never been abused or run low on oil; the 9A1 flat-six is a strong motor but a bad one is a five-figure problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Bore scoring / cylinder scuffing on the 9A1 DFI flat-six is uncommon but not extinct, and it is the single catastrophic risk. Symptoms are ticking or knocking at cold start that fades as it warms, oil consumption worse than roughly 1 qt / 1,200 miles, and a faint sooty smell. It shows up most often on hard-driven or short-tripped cars past 60-80k miles. A borescope of all six cylinders plus a DME over-rev report is the only real protection; an engine replacement or rebuild is $18,000-$28,000+.', 'Cracked cylinder heads / coolant loss on early 9A1 engines (mostly 2013-2014) present as slow, unexplained coolant level drop with no visible external leak, sometimes with a sweet smell after a hard drive. Check the expansion tank level history in service records and pressure-test the cooling system. Head or engine work is $8,000-$20,000.', 'Water pump with a composite impeller typically fails between 60k and 100k miles or roughly 8-10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump area, coolant smell, or temperature creep in traffic. Budget $1,100-$1,800 done properly with a thermostat and coolant service. On a 78k-mile 2014 with no pump record, assume it is due.', 'Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age, and the plastic coolant hard lines / hose connectors get brittle. Look for dried pink-orange crust in the engine bay and at the rear of the block. $400-$900.', 'Air-oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure causes a big puff of blue smoke at startup or after a highway pull, rough idle, and oil consumption. Typical at 70k-100k miles; $700-$1,200 installed. Frequently misdiagnosed as bore scoring, so a proper crankcase vacuum test is worth insisting on.', 'Rear main seal and, less often, the case-half seam weep oil onto the transaxle bellhousing. A light film is common; drips that require topping off mean pulling the transaxle, which is a $2,000-$3,500 job unless combined with a clutch.', 'Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch. Judder from a stop, high engagement point, or a rattle at idle that disappears with the clutch depressed means DMF. Replacement with flywheel and rear main seal while you are in there runs $3,000-$4,500. Most 981 manuals go 80k-120k miles, so a 78k car is inside the window.', 'PDK cars: the 60k-mile / 6-year mechatronic fluid and filter service is $700-$1,100 and is skipped constantly. A missing PDK service record on a 70k+ car is a real negotiating point; mechatronic unit failure is $5,000-$9,000.', 'Convertible top: the drive cables, hydraulic pump lines, tensioning bow bushings, microswitches, and the rear window seam are all wear items. Symptoms are a top that stalls mid-cycle, a warning message, or a hydraulic fluid smell/stain in the rear trunk area. Cable or hydraulic repairs run $1,200-$2,500; a full top replacement is $2,800-$4,500. Always cycle the top three or four times, fully, before buying.', "Clogged convertible-top and cowl drains flood the footwells and the area under the seats where control modules live. Look for damp carpet padding, musty smell, corroded seat rail hardware, or a car with a recent 'electrical gremlin' history. Water-damaged modules are $800-$2,500 each.", 'PASM dampers (standard on S/GTS, optional on base) start weeping and losing damping between 70k and 100k miles; you get a chassis warning or clunking over expansion joints. OEM dampers are $700-$1,300 per corner installed. Aftermarket coilovers on a listing usually mean the originals were tired.', 'A/C condensers sit in the front corners behind the radiators and collect leaves, sand, and salt; in a coastal environment they corrode and leak refrigerant, and the same debris rots the radiators. Expect $900-$1,800 to replace condensers and clean the ducting. Ask for photos of the front corner ducts with the liners out.', 'Bi-xenon / PDLS headlight units and ballasts fail with age and are expensive: $1,200-$2,200 per side for OEM. A car with recently replaced headlights (as in this example) has already eaten that cost, w
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid catch-up: engine oil with genuine filter, brake fluid flush (2-year interval, almost always overdue), coolant condition check and pressure test', 'Tires: replace non-N-spec or over-5-year-old staggered set with N-rated rubber, plus alignment ($1,600-$2,200)', 'Cooling system: water pump and thermostat if there is no record within 60k miles ($1,100-$1,800)', 'Convertible top service: lubricate mechanism, clear cowl and top drains, check hydraulic lines and rear window seam ($300-$700, more if cables are stretched)', 'Battery test/replace with proper coding if the car sat or is on its original AGM ($400-$600)', 'Exhaust: verify smog compliance for California registration; source and reinstall factory exhaust if cats were deleted ($1,200-$2,500)', 'PIWIS fault-code clear and re-s
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on a manual approaching 90-100k miles ($3,000-$4,500) or PDK mechatronic service if not documented ($700-$1,100)', 'Air-oil separator if oil consumption or startup smoke develops ($700-$1,200)', 'PASM damper replacement if weeping or if ride quality is degraded ($2,800-$4,500 for four)', 'A/C condenser replacement and front duct cleanout, typical for coastal cars ($900-$1,800)', 'Spark plugs and coils at the 4-year/40k interval ($600-$1,000)', 'Engine and transmission mounts if idle shudder is present ($600-$1,200)', 'Soft-top rear window or full top replacement if the seam is delaminating ($2,800-$4,500)', 'Suspension refresh items: control arm bushings, sway bar links, and a corner-balance alignment ($800-$1,600)']
profiles.market_notes: Transmission and engine drive the money: a 6-speed manual commands a clear premium over PDK in the enthusiast market, and Boxster S / GTS 3.4 cars trade several thousand above a 2.7 base regardless of options. Spec matters at the margins - Sport Chrono with PSE, adaptive sport seats, PASM, a non-black interior, and a genuinely interesting exterior color lift a car; base cloth-spec silver/white/black cars with 19s and no options sit. Records are worth real money on this generation: a folder showing water pump, PDK or clutch service, brake fluid history, and no accidents will beat a lower-mileage undocumented car with a damage entry. Aftermarket exhaust, non-N-spec tires, and a Carfax damage report each shave value, and mileage bands break roughly at 40k, 70k, and 100k.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-12 year old, 70-80k mile 981 needs a deferred-maintenance sweep even when it looks perfect: brake fluid, coolant, plugs and coils, AGM battery with coding, water pump if undocumented, N-spec tires, and a convertible top lubrication and drain cleanout. Coastal Monterey cars additionally want the front duct liners pulled to clean debris off the radiators and condensers before corrosion sets in. Plan $3,000-$5,000 of catch-up in the first year on top of the purchase price, separate from the clutch/DMF or PDK service that lurks in the next 20k miles.

Borescope images of all six cylinders showing no scoring (a bonus when present; not having one is not held against the car, policy 1.9.2)

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster / Boxster S (987.1 & 987.2)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 987 is a mid-engine, open-top back-road car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the occasional track day — not a garage investment. It is one of the last analog, hydraulically-assisted Porsches available at commuter-car money, and a well-documented manual example is a genuinely usable daily driver with a frunk plus trunk. The entire buying decision hinges on engine provenance: 987.1 cars (2005–2008, M96/M97) carry IMS bearing and bore-scoring risk that can turn a $16k car into a $30k car overnight, while 987.2 cars (2009–2012, 9A1 DFI) eliminate both. Coastal humidity and salt air matter less than rust-belt exposure, but clogged convertible-top and cowl drains cause expensive electrical damage in any climate.
profiles.weak_points: 1) IMS bearing (2005–2008 M96/M97 only): 2005 and very early 2006 engines use the smaller single-row bearing with the highest failure rate; engines built from roughly mid-2006 through 2008 use a larger non-serviceable bearing with a lower failure rate but which cannot be retrofitted without splitting the engine. A proactive IMS retrofit (LN Engineering ceramic hybrid or IMS Solution) done with clutch and RMS runs $3,000–$4,500 and should be documented by invoice with the engine number. Absence of a retrofit is not a dealbreaker on a 2006+ car but is a $3.5k line item. 2) Bore scoring: most common on the 3.4 M97 (2007–2008 S) but present on 2.7s too; symptoms are cold-start rattle/ticking that fades, elevated oil consumption (worse than ~1 qt/1,000 mi), and a smoky start after sitting. Only a borescope through the spark plug holes proves cylinder condition — this is the single most valuable pre-purchase test. A scored engine means a $12,000–$20,000 rebuild or used-engine swap. 3) Rear main seal (RMS) weeping: nearly universal at some level; a light film is normal, active dripping onto the bellhousing means $1,500–$2,000 alone or fold it into a clutch/IMS job. 4) Air/oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure at 60k–100k miles: huge white smoke cloud at startup, rough idle, oil pulled into intake; $600–$1,200 installed. 5) Water pump with plastic impeller: typical life 60k–80k miles; impeller blades shed and clog the system, $700–$1,100. Do it with the thermostat and coolant. 6) Coolant expansion tank cracks and cap failure at 10–15 years, $700–$1,200; look for dried pink/orange crust in the engine bay and under the rear. 7) Front radiators and A/C condensers: leaves and debris pack the lower ducts, holding moisture against aluminum until the condensers corrode through — extremely common on 12–20 year old cars. Full front radiator/condenser refresh with grilles is $1,500–$2,800. 8) Convertible top: transmission cables fray and the plastic drive blocks/rollers break, the hydraulic pump and rams leak onto the trunk carpet, the microswitches and the rear window seam fail. Top mechanism work is $1,000–$2,500; a new top with window is $2,000–$3,500. 9) Blocked top and cowl drains: water backs up into the footwells and into the seat/convertible-top control modules and under-seat wiring — causes dash warnings, dead tops, and mildew. Pull the carpet edges and check for staining. 10) Suspension wear at 70k+ miles: front lower control arms (including the rear 'coffin' arm bushings), front and rear top mounts, and tie rods; a full corner refresh is $1,500–$3,000. Sagging ride height and clunks over expansion joints are the tell. 11) Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on 100k-mile manuals: $2,500–$3,500 done properly with RMS and IMS access. Judder from a stop is the DMF. 12) Variocam actuators/solenoids and chain-pad wear on M96/M97: a rattle for 1–3 seconds on cold start plus cam deviation values out of spec on a Durametric scan; actuator/solenoid work $1,200–$2,500. 13) Electrical annoyances: ignition switch failure, door lock/latch microswitches (door won't unlock, top won't operate), airbag light from the passenger seat occupancy mat ($600–$1,000 for the mat), and PCM2 unit/CD-changer failures. 14) Tiptronic (5-speed auto in 987.1) and PDK (987.2): the Tiptronic is durable but dulls the car badly and hurts resale; PDK mechatronic and clutch-pack service is expensive out of warranty ($3,000+). 987.2 DFI engines are far more robust but are known for occasional high-pressure fuel pump and injector issues and for coolant-pipe/thermostat housing seepage.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluids service (Mobil 1 0W-40 with a genuine filter, brake fluid, coolant top-up), four correct-size tires if mismatched or over 6 years old, front radiator/condenser duct cleaning and grille installation, convertible-top and cowl drain clearing, serpentine belt and tensioner if undocumented, battery if unknown age, and an alignment. Budget $1,200–$2,500. If the borescope or oil filter cut shows anything marginal, stop and renegotiate rather than repairing.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if there is no receipt in the last 60k miles, AOS if there is any startup smoke or idle hunt, coolant expansion tank on any 15+ year old car, front control arms and top mounts, a clutch/DMF plus IMS retrofit combined job on a 987.1 approaching 100k miles, convertible top transmission cables or hydraulic ram seals, and typically one electrical gremlin (ignition switch, door latch microswitch, or seat occupancy mat). Realistic 12-month spend on an unsorted 2006: $3,000–$6,000.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission is worth a clear premium over Tiptronic and is close to mandatory for resale; S models (3.2 then 3.4) carry roughly a 15–25% premium over base 2.7s, and 987.2 DFI cars command a further step up because they have no IMS and no meaningful bore-scoring reputation. Documented IMS retrofit, recent clutch, and a clean borescope report can add $2,000–$4,000 of buyer confidence on a 987.1. Color and options move money more than mileage below 100k: Guards Red, Cobalt/Aqua Blue, Speed Yellow and GT Silver with sport seats, PASM, Sport Chrono, litronics and a hardtop sell fastest, while black-on-black base cars with automatics are the soft end. Boxster Spyder and RS 60 Spyder trade in their own, much higher tier.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 15–20 year old 987.1 arrives needing rubber and plastic more than metal: coolant expansion tank, water pump, AOS, serpentine belt and tensioner, engine and top-mechanism seals, convertible-top cables and drain hoses, and front suspension bushings — plus tires and brake fluid regardless of tread and pedal feel. Assume $2,500–$4,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year even on a nicely kept car, and treat any clutch job as the right moment to bundle IMS, RMS, and flywheel work.

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster S (986, 2000-2004)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 986 Boxster S is an affordable mid-engine roadster for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and Laureles Grade. It is a driver, not an appreciating asset. Nearly the whole purchase decision comes down to verifiable engine health: IMS bearing status, DME over-rev history, oil filter debris and cylinder condition, because an engine failure can cost more than the car is worth. After that, prioritize a documented cooling system, a sound top that keeps out coastal fog and rain, and a clean structural history. Cosmetic wear is cheap to live with; an undocumented engine is not.
profiles.weak_points: ["Intermediate shaft (IMS) bearing. Early engines (MY2000 to roughly early MY2001) mostly used the stronger dual-row bearing. The 2002-2004 cars, including the 2003 example, use the single-row bearing, which has a meaningfully higher failure rate. The failure is often sudden: metal in the oil filter, cam deviation codes, then chain and valve destruction, and a used or rebuilt engine runs about $10,000-20,000. The fix is a retrofit, LN Engineering IMS Retrofit (ceramic hybrid) or IMS Solution (plain bearing), ideally done alongside a clutch job for about $3,000-4,500 all-in. Seller claims of 'IMS done' with no invoice should be treated as not done. Require an invoice naming the part, the mileage and the shop. A photo of the removed bearing and LN's engine-bay sticker help corroborate it.", 'Rear main seal (RMS) and IMS flange leaks at the engine-transmission junction. These are very common on the M96. A light seep is tolerable, but an active drip or oil on the clutch is not. Standalone repair is about $1,500-2,500 because the transmission must come out, so it is normally done with the clutch and IMS. Look for a recent RMS invoice and check the bellhousing seam from below.', 'Over-rev and mechanical over-rev (money shift). The DME logs ignition counts in rev ranges 1-6. Ranges 1-3 are mostly harmless (fuel cut), but significant counts in ranges 4-6 indicate a mis-shift such as 5th to 2nd. That raises the risk of bent valves, chain and guide damage, or rod bearing stress. Read it with PIWIS or Durametric, and note the total operating hours so you can judge how far back the log goes.', 'Cam timing deviation and timing chain wear. Worn chain tensioner pads and guides, or a slipped VarioCam adjuster, show up as cam deviation values outside spec, typically beyond about ±6°, or bank-to-bank mismatch. They also appear as P1341-family codes and as a rattle on cold start. Tensioner pads and guides are roughly $1,500-3,500. Cam deviation is also an early warning of IMS trouble.', "Bore scoring, cracked or slipped cylinder liners, and porous blocks. These are less common on the 986's 3.2 than on later 3.4/3.6/3.8 engines, but they are not rare at this age and mileage. Symptoms are a sooty single tailpipe on one bank, rising oil consumption (more than about 1 qt/1,000 mi), a ticking that does not go away when warm, and oil mixed into coolant from the 'D-chunk' liner crack. A borescope inspection costs about $150-300 and is the only real test. A rebuild is $12,000-20,000.", 'Air-oil separator (AOS). It fails as a cloud of white or blue smoke on cold start, a rough or hunting idle, high crankcase vacuum (oil filler cap hard to remove at idle), oil in the intake and throttle body, and lean codes (P0171/P0174). Replacement is about $400-900 in parts and labor. A badly failed AOS can hydrolock the engine with oil.', 'Cooling system. The coolant expansion tank cracks and seeps at its seams (about $400-700). The water pump impeller and bearing wear out (about $700-1,200 with thermostat, preventively every 50-60k miles or about 6 years). Bypass and heater hoses age. Coolant smell in the cabin or engine bay, pink crust on the tank, or a low reservoir are red flags. Records should show a water pump and thermostat within the last 60k miles or 6 years.', 'Front radiators, condensers and the S-specific center radiator. They sit behind front openings that trap leaves and debris, which hold moisture and corrode the fins. In salty, foggy Carmel air this accelerates. Expect AC failure and higher coolant temperatures. Condensers run about $200-400 each in parts, radiators about $300-500 each, plus about $400-800 labor. Plan on yearly cleaning with the bumper off.', 'Ignition coils and spark plug tubes. Coils crack with heat cycles and cause misfires (P0300-P0306), about $60-90 each. Leaking spark plug tube O-rings and VarioCam solenoid seals let oil into the plug wells. Check the coil boots for oil and look for a dated plug and coil invoice. Plugs are due ab

profiles.market_notes: The 6-speed manual Boxster S commands a clear premium over the 5-speed Tiptronic. The 2003-2004 facelift cars (glass rear window, glovebox, revised bumpers and lights) are preferred, and the 2004 550 Spyder 50th Anniversary sits in its own collector tier well above regular S cars. A documented IMS retrofit with recent clutch/RMS work and thorough records can add roughly $2,000-4,000, while a reported accident, undocumented engine work or rebuilt title knock values down hard. Desirable options (Sport package, LSD, 18-inch wheels, interesting colors like Speed Yellow, Guards Red or Lapis Blue) help modestly. Mileage under about 60k earns a premium but is not a proxy for IMS health, since low-use cars can be more at risk.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 20+ year-old 986 S with patchy records needs a cooling system refresh (water pump, thermostat, tank), AOS, plugs and coils, and belts. It also usually needs suspension bushings and springs, radiator/condenser cleaning or replacement, and top service, which together run roughly $3,000-6,000 before any IMS or clutch work. Budget an additional $3,000-4,500 for IMS, clutch and RMS if none is documented.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayenne S (958.1, 2011–2014)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 958.1 Cayenne S is the do-everything Carmel car: a 400hp naturally aspirated 4.8 V8 with a genuinely good 8-speed Tiptronic, air suspension, all-wheel drive, and enough room for dogs, luggage, and a Highway 1 weekend. It is not an investment — depreciation has already done its work, and these trade around $15k–$25k regardless of how nice they are — so the whole game is buying the cheapest possible future maintenance rather than the cheapest possible car. A documented, one- or two-owner, non-air-suspension-failing example with cooling, suspension, and driveline receipts is worth a $5,000 premium over a bargain car, because that is roughly the delta in first-year repairs. Rust is a non-issue in coastal California; deferred German maintenance is the entire risk.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Coolant pipe / thermostat housing and water pump: the 4.8 V8's plastic coolant distribution components and the water pump are wear items typically due by 80–100k miles. Symptoms are low coolant warnings, sweet smell after shutdown, and crusty orange residue at the front/valley of the engine. Water pump plus thermostat runs $1,200–$2,200; a coolant pipe or crossover job that requires intake removal can hit $3,000+. Look for a receipt naming 'water pump' and 'thermostat' within the last 40k miles.

2) Air suspension (standard on most S cars, as on this example): rubber air struts crack with age/ozone and the compressor then runs itself to death trying to keep up. Symptoms are the car sitting low or nose-down overnight, 'Level Control Fault / Chassis Malfunction' messages, or the compressor audibly running at every start. OE Porsche struts are $1,200–$1,800 each installed; a compressor and valve block is $700–$1,200; a full four-corner refresh can exceed $6,000. On a 2011–2014 car that has never had struts replaced, assume this is a when-not-if item. Ask for the overnight ride-height video and any struts/compressor invoices.

3) Transfer case (the 958's biggest sleeper cost): the electronically controlled multi-plate clutch transfer case wears its clutch pack and servo motor, typically 70–120k miles. Symptoms are binding or shudder in tight low-speed turns, a 'PSM/4WD Failure' or 'Transfer Case Fault' message, driveline clunk, or a stored fault for the servo. Porsche does not rebuild it — a new unit is $4,000–$6,500 installed, and rebuild specialists run $2,500–$3,500. Mismatched or badly worn tires accelerate failure; check that all four tires are the same brand, model, and within ~2/32" of each other.

4) Driveshaft center support bearing and flex discs: a hum or vibration at 45–70 mph or a shudder from a stop. The driveshaft is often sold as a complete assembly; $1,200–$2,200 installed.

5) Rear differential and rear cover/bushing leaks, plus the Cayenne's habit of weeping from the transfer case output seal onto the rear driveshaft. Wipe the underside and look for fresh wet fluid versus old dry film.

6) 4.8 V8 oil consumption and valve cover / cam cover gasket seepage: some consumption is normal (up to ~1qt/1,000 mi Porsche considers acceptable), but heavy consumption with blue puff on cold start can indicate bore scoring on high-mile or hard-used examples. Bore scoring is rare on the 958 N/A 4.8 compared with the 955/957 era but not unheard of; a borescope of cylinders during PPI is cheap insurance and a scored engine is a $12,000+ walk-away.

7) Direct injection carbon buildup on intake valves: 80k+ cars often show rough cold idle, misfire codes at light load, and reduced mid-range. Walnut blasting is $900–$1,600 and is not in most service histories — treat as likely-due if there's no record.

8) Starter, alternator, and the buried-under-the-intake serviceability tax: nearly everything on the V8 top end requires intake removal, so labor multiplies. A starter that would be $400 on a Toyota is $1,200–$1,800 here.

9) PCM/electronics: the 2011–2014 PCM 3.1 head units suffer dead nav discs/SD readers, failed Bose amp channels, and delaminating touchscreens. Also check the panoramic/regular sunroof drains and the rear hatch strut/power liftgate motor. Aftermarket head unit swaps are common and often hide a failed OE unit.

10) Front suspension bushings and control arms: thrust arm and lower control arm bushings go 70–110k miles, producing clunks over expansion joints and wandering. Full front arms both sides $1,400–$2,400.

11) Brakes: 958 rotors are large and tend to crack around the vents and lip on stop-start use; a full four-corner rotor and pad job with sensors is $1,800–$3,000 at OE, less with quality aftermarket. Check rotor thickness and edge lip, not just pad life.

12) 21" wheels (as on the example car) with 295/35 tires: harsh ride, bent-rim risk on bad pavement, and a $1,600–$2,400 tire bill every 25–30k miles. Cu
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, brake fluid, coolant condition check, transfer case and differential fluids, Tiptronic fluid and filter if no record); battery test and replacement with registration; four matched tires if the set is mismatched or aged past 6 years; fresh alignment; sunroof drain flush; likely front thrust-arm bushings or a rattling sway bar link; wiper blades, cabin filter, engine air filters. Budget $2,000–$4,000 in the first 30 days on a typical 80k-mile example, more if the tire set must be replaced.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not documented in the last 40k miles; one or two air struts and quite possibly the compressor and relay; walnut blasting for intake carbon; brake rotors and pads at all four corners; driveshaft center support bearing if a 50–70 mph hum is present; front lower control arms; possible transfer case service or replacement if any low-speed binding was noted at PPI. Realistic 12-month range for a well-bought car is $3,500–$7,000; a neglected one can double that.
profiles.market_notes: The 958.1 Cayenne S sits in a narrow $14k–$26k band where condition and records matter far more than options — clean-Carfax, two-owner, California cars with a service binder and no air-suspension faults live at the top, and any 'sold as-is with lights on' car lands at the bottom regardless of spec. The S (4.8 V8) is the sweet spot: better sound and simpler than the Turbo, dramatically more desirable than the V6 base, and without the Hybrid's battery risk; the rare 958.1 Cayenne S with a manual is a curiosity, not a value driver here. Color and interior move money modestly — white/black/grey over black or cognac sells easiest, and an unusual combination like Cream and Umber with birch trim adds interest but narrows the buyer pool. 21" wheels look good and cost money; smaller 18"/19" wheels are arguably a value-add for a real-world driver, and documented recent air struts, water pump, or transfer case work is worth more than any option code.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 10–14 year old, 80k-mile 958.1 is due for essentially everything the factory called 'lifetime': transmission fluid and filter, transfer case and differential fluids, coolant, brake fluid, and usually a battery. Rubber-based systems — air struts, control arm bushings, coolant hoses, engine mounts — age out on calendar rather than mileage, so even a low-mile California car should be budgeted as if it had 90k on it.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayenne Turbo (955, 4.5L twin-turbo V8)
profiles.framing: This is a 450-hp, 5,200-lb German luxury SUV that now trades for beater-Camry money precisely because the deferred maintenance bill can exceed the purchase price. For a Carmel-based buyer it makes sense only as a cheap, capable, weather-proof second vehicle — Highway 1 in the rain, Sierra ski trips, Big Sur fire roads — bought with eyes open and a funded repair reserve, never as an economy car. What matters is not the odometer but whether the coolant pipes, driveshaft, air suspension and propshaft/transfer case work has already been done with paper to prove it; a 47k-mile untouched example is arguably riskier than a 110k-mile one with a documented pipe job. Low mileage on a 20-year-old 955 mostly means aged rubber, plastic and seals, not a young car.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Plastic coolant crossover pipes under the intake manifold (the defining 955 Turbo failure). The factory used glued plastic Y-pipes and coolant tubes in the valley; they embrittle with heat cycling and let go — sometimes catastrophically at speed, which can cook the alloy block. Symptoms are coolant smell, weeping from the two telltale drain holes at the bellhousing, and low-coolant warnings. The fix is aluminum replacement pipes (Pelican/Sharkwerks/Dansk-style kits), $2,500–$4,500 with intake and turbo plumbing off; on a Turbo it is more labor than on an NA. Look for an invoice with line items for 'coolant pipes,' 'valley pipes,' or 'aluminum coolant tube upgrade,' plus photos taken with the intake off. No borescope, no invoice = assume it's due. 2) Driveshaft (propshaft) center support bearing and flex joints, typically 60k–100k miles or by age. Vibration at 40–60 mph, clunk on throttle transitions. Porsche sells only the complete shaft; $1,500–$2,500 installed, or rebuilt center bearing by a specialist for $600–$1,000. 3) Transfer case — the 955's electronically shifted case with dual-range and variable center diff. The servo motor and internal chain/clutch wear; symptoms are 'Transfer Case Fault' or 'Low Range Fault' in the dash, ABS/PSM lights, driveline binding, or a case that won't leave low. Servo motor rebuild $400–$900; complete used/reman case $2,000–$4,500 installed. Fluid is 'lifetime' and almost never changed — ask for it. 4) Air suspension: rear air springs and front struts crack and leak (car sits down overnight or on one corner), compressor then runs itself to death, and the valve block/level sensors fail. Individual bag $500–$900 per corner installed; compressor $500–$1,200; a full corner-by-corner rehab easily $3,000+. PASM shocks are separate and expensive. 5) Turbo/exhaust side: cracked exhaust manifolds and broken manifold-to-turbo studs on 4.5 twin-turbos, plus turbo oil-return leaks and wastegate/vacuum actuator faults. Blue smoke on startup, boost under-target codes, ticking cold. Manifold/stud work $1,500–$3,000; a turbo cartridge or pair $3,000–$6,000+. 6) Ignition and secondary air: eight coils and plugs are a wear item every ~60k or 10 years ($600–$1,000); secondary air injection pump and combi-valves stick and set P0410-family codes that will fail smog in California ($700–$1,800). 7) Cardan/front differential and front axle output seals leak; the front diff mounting bushings on the sump can allow diff movement. 8) Cooling accessories: thermostat housing, water pump (composite impeller), radiator end tanks and the plastic coolant reservoir all age out at 15–20 years; budget $1,200–$2,500 as a package if none of it is documented. 9) Electrical gremlins from the twin batteries/alternator and corroded grounds — the 955 is very voltage-sensitive and a weak battery produces a Christmas tree of faults (PSM, transfer case, air suspension) that clear with a good battery. A July 2023 battery on a car that sits is already suspect. 10) Interior: sticky soft-touch coatings on switchgear and the center console, sagging headliner, failed PCM/CD units, non-functioning HVAC blend-motor clicking, and cracked dash tops. Aftermarket head units (like a Dynavin) often mean a factory PCM failed or the CAN-integrated OEM unit was ripped out — check that the radio removal didn't break OBC/telephone functions. 11) Brakes: 350mm+ rotors and huge pads, $1,200–$2,000 for four corners with rotors; low-mileage cars almost always have rust-pitted or warped rotors from sitting. 12) Tires and alignment: a 20-year-old low-mile car will have date-coded-out rubber regardless of tread; a lifted, small-wheel, all-terrain conversion like this listing needs a fresh alignment and can throw PSM/ride-height calibration off. 13) Fuel economy and consumables are genuinely brutal — 13–15 mpg real world on premium, and the Turbo's parts pricing is 911 money on a 5,200-lb truck. 14) On lifted/off-road-converted cars, verify the air suspension
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, coolant if unknown, transfer case, front and rear diff, brake fluid, power steering, ZF Tiptronic service if no record) $900–$1,800. New battery and a proper charging-system/parasitic-draw check $300–$500. Four new date-coded tires and an alignment $1,100–$1,600. Full diagnostic scan on PIWIS/Durametric across all modules with printout, plus a borescope look at the valley coolant pipes if no invoice exists. Brake rotors and pads front and rear on a sat-a-lot car $1,200–$2,000. Air suspension leak-down test and likely at least one air spring $600–$1,000. Spark plugs and any weeping coils if older than 10 years $600–$1,000. On a modified example, either revert the lift/bumper to stock or budget the labor to verify fitment, ride-height calibration and sensor f
profiles.repairs_12mo: Coolant pipe conversion to aluminum if not already documented $2,500–$4,500. Driveshaft center bearing or complete shaft $800–$2,500. Thermostat, water pump, reservoir and hoses as an age-based package $1,200–$2,500. Secondary air pump/valves to pass California smog $700–$1,800. Transfer case servo or fluid-and-inspect, with reman case as the tail risk $500–$4,500. Air suspension compressor and remaining corners $1,000–$3,000. Exhaust manifold studs/gaskets and turbo oil-line seals $1,000–$3,000. Suspension bushings, control arms and sway bar links from age $1,000–$2,000. Interior fixes: headliner, sticky-plastic switchgear, HVAC blend motors $500–$1,500.
profiles.market_notes: 955 Turbos are near the bottom of their depreciation curve — running, sorted examples trade roughly $8k–$16k, with unsorted or high-mileage cars at $4k–$8k and exceptional low-mile documented cars occasionally to $20k+; Turbo S and the rare late-955 cars carry a modest premium. Price is driven almost entirely by documentation of the big-ticket items (coolant pipes, driveshaft, transfer case, air suspension) rather than by mileage; a $6k car with none of that work is a $12k car in disguise. Manual transmission was never offered on the Turbo, so Tiptronic is correct and not a demerit. Overland/lift conversions narrow the buyer pool and add unknowns — stock, unmodified, well-optioned (PCM, comfort seats, factory air suspension in good order) cars in conservative colors over black or stone gray sell best; California cars avoid the corroded fastener and rusty subframe misery of salt states and are worth seeking out.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any 955 Turbo as a 20-year-old car first and a low-mileage car second: rubber, plastic, coolant-system components and seals age out on a calendar, not an odometer, so a 47k-mile untouched example needs the same coolant pipes, hoses, air springs, tires and fluids as a 120k-mile one. Plan on $4,000–$8,000 of catch-up in the first year even on a clean, running example, and buy at a price that leaves that headroom.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayenne Turbo (957, 4.8L Twin-Turbo V8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 957 Turbo is a cheap-to-buy, expensive-to-keep family hauler that happens to do 0-60 in 4.7 seconds and tow 7,700 lbs — a Monterey-Peninsula daily that can run Highway 1, haul dogs and bikes, and still handle a dirt road to a trailhead. The purchase price is now the smallest number in the ownership equation: a $20k car with $10k of deferred air suspension, PDCC, coolant, transfer case and brake work is a bad deal, while a $35k car with a documented $15k of that work already done is usually the cheaper car. Because the buyer wants documented and unmodified examples, lifted/light-barred/cat-deleted trucks are a poor fit — especially in California, where a 2008 gasoline Cayenne needs a biennial smog check and a change-of-ownership smog on initial registration. The right example is a two-owner, Porsche- or independent-specialist-serviced car with a thick folder, stock ride height, working air suspension and PDCC, and no overheating in its history.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Cooling system plumbing. The 4.8L (M48.50) fixed the notorious 4.5L plastic coolant pipes but replaced them with its own set of failure points: the plastic thermostat housing and coolant crossover/distribution pieces in the valley, the plastic-impeller water pump, and the rear coolant 'Y'. Typical failure window is 60k–100k miles or 10+ years; symptoms are sweet smell, low-coolant messages, and pink crust at the front of the valley or behind the alternator. Water pump + thermostat housing + hoses runs $1,800–3,500 with labor; a valley-pipe job or one done with the intake off can reach $4,000+. Look for a receipt naming water pump, thermostat housing, and coolant pipes — and confirm no head-gasket or overheat episode preceded it.

2) Crankcase ventilation (AOS/vent hoses). The molded crankcase vent hoses go brittle and collapse or split, causing rough idle, a whistle, oil consumption, and misfire/lean codes. Parts are cheap, labor is not: $600–1,500. Nearly every 100k-mile car needs this once.

3) Turbochargers and boost plumbing. Wastegate rattle, coked bearings after hot shutdowns, and cracked/leaking pressure pipes and diverter valves. A pair of factory turbos is $7,000–12,000 installed; rebuilds $4,000–6,000. Blue smoke on startup or after coasting, a shrill whine, or boost-deviation codes (P0299/P0234) are walk-away territory unless priced in. Ask for an oil-consumption figure per 1,000 miles and any boost-leak test results.

4) Direct injection carbon buildup. The 4.8L DFI V8 cokes its intake valves; by 80k–120k miles expect rough cold idle and misfires. Walnut blasting is $900–1,800. Coils and plugs are a routine 60k item ($600–1,200 for eight of each).

5) Air suspension. Rear air springs and front struts leak (car sits down overnight, 'Level control system fault'), the compressor burns out from chasing leaks, the valve block sticks, and ride-height sensors fail. OEM front strut $1,100–1,800 each, rear bag $500–900 each, compressor $700–1,400, all installed. A car that hasn't had at least a compressor and one or two corners done by 120k miles is due. Aftermarket lift kits and adjustable control arms fight the level-control calibration and wear ball joints/CV boots fast.

6) PDCC (Porsche Dynamic Chassis Control). Hydraulic active anti-roll bars — pump, lines, and bar actuators leak; a failed system throws a chassis warning and cannot be cheaply deleted. Repairs commonly land $2,500–6,000. If the listing mentions PDCC, demand evidence the system holds pressure and shows no faults.

7) Transfer case / AWD unit. The 957's transfer case chain stretches and the range/clutch actuator servo fails: symptoms are a grind or clunk on tight turns, 'Transfer case fault — 4WD limited,' or driveline shudder. Replacement transfer case is $3,500–6,000; this is the single most common big-dollar surprise on high-mile cars.

8) Driveshaft (cardan) center bearing and flex discs. Vibration at 40–70 mph or a shudder from a stop. Shaft replacement $1,200–2,500; some shops rebuild the center bearing for less.

9) Transmission (Aisin TR-60SN 6-speed). Durable if serviced, but Porsche called the fluid 'lifetime.' Neglected units show torque-converter shudder, 2-3 flare, or limp mode. Fluid, filter and pan service is $700–1,100; a rebuild/replacement is $5,000–8,000. Also common: the shifter/park-position (gear selector) switch failing to recognize Park — the example listing's exact complaint — a $400–900 fix but a tow-truck event when it strands you.

10) Secondary air injection. P0410/P0491-92 from a failed SAI pump or clogged passages; pump $600–1,200. A live smog-check concern in California.

11) Brakes. Turbo six-piston fronts with big rotors: a full four-corner pad-and-rotor job is $2,200–4,000 with OEM parts, and warped/lipped rotors are common on a car used as a mall SUV. Check for the rear electric parking-brake actuator and cable corrosion.

12) Emissions hardware. Secondary-cat bypass pipes, aftermarket downpipes, or missing cats mea
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up on almost any example: engine oil, transmission fluid/filter/pan gasket, transfer case fluid, front and rear diff fluid, brake fluid, coolant (~$1,500–2,500 total). Expect an air-suspension leak to surface within weeks (one strut/bag plus compressor, $1,200–2,500). Crankcase vent hoses and a vacuum-leak smoke test ($600–1,500). Coils/plugs and air filters if not receipted in the last 40k miles ($700–1,400). Tires — most of these cars wear staggered 265/50-19 or 275/45-20 and need a matched set of four for the AWD system ($1,400–2,200). Alignment after any suspension work. Fix any Park-position/shifter switch fault before it leaves you stranded. For a California-bound car: restore factory catalysts and stock ride height as needed to pass smog and referee, if the car has
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump, thermostat housing and accessible coolant pipes if not already documented ($1,800–3,500). Walnut-blast intake valves ($900–1,800). Brakes all around on a Turbo ($2,200–4,000). Remaining air-suspension corners and ride-height sensors ($1,500–3,000). Front control arm bushings, tie rods, and sway bar links ($1,200–2,500). Driveshaft center bearing or flex discs if any 40–70 mph vibration ($1,200–2,500). Serpentine belt, tensioner, pulleys, battery and battery-management reset. Budget the transfer case as a probable within-two-years item on anything past 120k miles ($3,500–6,000). Miscellaneous: sunroof drains, door latch actuator, tailgate struts, PCM/camera quirks.
profiles.market_notes: 957 Turbos have bottomed out and trade largely on records and mileage rather than spec: sub-80k-mile, single-dealer-serviced cars with air suspension and PDCC working bring $28k–45k, while 120k+ mile examples with thin history land in the high teens to mid-$20s — the example's $22,000 for a 137k-mile modified car is market-correct, not a bargain. Documentation of the expensive jobs (coolant/water pump, air struts, transfer case, turbos) is worth more than low mileage without paperwork. Turbo S and rare colors/interiors (Chestnut Brown or natural leather, Meteor Grey, GTS-style options) carry a small premium; black-on-black high-mile cars are the floor. Off-road builds, lift kits, light bars and cat bypasses actively reduce the pool of buyers and are a liability in California.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 15-plus-year-old 957 Turbo needs age-based work regardless of mileage: every rubber coolant and vacuum hose, the crankcase vent plumbing, plastic thermostat housing, air-spring bellows, control arm bushings, tires (date codes matter more than tread), battery and battery-management, and all drivetrain fluids. Budget $4,000–7,000 of catch-up in year one on a good example and treat the transfer case, air struts, and turbos as scheduled future expenses rather than surprises.
